Would get interested again if the market cap pulled back meaningfully.
Lithium Universe (LU7) Neutral 00:55:17
  • Craig likes the precious-metal recycling/recovery technology (especially the silver-recovery process) as a standalone business, but is frustrated the company keeps chasing a ~A$1B+ lithium hydroxide refinery that an ~$8M market-cap company has no realistic path to fund (prior DFS on the first refinery showed only ~21% pretax IRR / 4-year payback) — and is now studying a second refinery on top of the unfunded first one.
  • Holds a binding offtake obligation to buy 80,000t/year of SC6 spodumene concentrate; without an operating refinery, plans to trade this on the spot market instead — a workable idea in theory, but funding for that trading position is unclear.
  • Craig's take: if management fully committed to the recycling business alone it could be a genuinely interesting company, but splitting focus between recycling and an unfundable refinery dream keeps it stuck at a depressed valuation.

Session Themes

  • Total addressable market size matters as much as demand growth — scandium's tiny (~US$1B), opaque global market means SRL's proposed production alone could flood supply and pressure prices, regardless of how attractive underlying demand looks (solid oxide fuel cells, scandium-aluminium alloys).
  • Government/strategic funding can reduce financing risk while simultaneously increasing technical risk, if the conditions attached push a company further downstream into harder, more capital-intensive processing than its original plan.
  • Re-assaying historical drill core with modern techniques (BKB/Shafter, S&M) is a recurring low-cost way to unlock previously "left on the table" polymetallic value, especially where old programs only assayed for one commodity.
  • Headline resource ounces need geometric context — a large total spread across many small, disconnected deposits (PTN) is fundamentally weaker than the same ounces in one coherent orebody.
  • Good management and execution (Develop Global's Bill Beament) earns a valuation premium, but Craig is explicit that paying for expected future success is different from buying at a genuine value entry point.
  • A credible, singular strategic identity matters for small caps — Lithium Universe's split focus between promising recycling tech and an unfundable refinery ambition was the clearest example of value being diluted by narrative confusion.

EXR Bearish 00:44:07

Session Themes

  • Distinguishing headline results from forward guidance trend is the recurring lens this session — CCP's slowing FY27/FY28 debt-buying pipeline versus its strong FY26 headline was the clearest example, explicitly compared to CSL's earnings-deceleration pattern.
  • For flow-rate/production-test announcements, go straight to the ASX-mandated compliance table (e.g., listing rule 5.3) rather than the promotional narrative text — applied to EXR's disappointing L3H well result.
  • Early-stage exploration (GBL) needs drill confirmation, not just rock chips, before it's genuinely investable — patience over headline grade excitement.
  • Known industry operators and financiers moving into a relisted/shell vehicle (Ray at GBL, LRT's stake) are treated as a forward-looking signal worth monitoring even before a company has real news flow.
  • Biotech catalysts (EMP's basket trial, NTI's ASD trial, SLD's device approval) were reviewed with attention to trial design/endpoints and commercialisation speed, not just headline drug names.

Fundamental Analysis Scan with Craig Dickson

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Tuesday 04 August 2026
Bullish Setups: BWN, Hammer Metals
Bearish Setups: CAY
Neutral / Watching: Hot Chili, FLG
CAY Bearish 00:09:36
  • Craig used CAY as a textbook example of takeover risk from a single dominant shareholder now holding roughly 55-70% of the register (combined with a related management holding).
  • That holder built its stake by bailing CAY out through cap raises and financing during past periods of weakness, then made a low (~$0.05) takeover offer after a share-price dump — well below the price that holder itself had been paying in.
  • A controlling holder that owns both equity and debt can block resolutions, force extra shareholder meetings, and starve liquidity, leaving minority holders with little real leverage.
  • Drew a parallel to Wyloo/Hastings, where a large debt-holder used that leverage to take control of a project, and flagged AIS as a company that narrowly avoided the same fate when institutions stepped in to refinance its debt at the last minute.
  • Takeaway: understand who controls both the equity register and the debt stack before investing in a concentrated-ownership company — that structure, not the headline, decides the outcome.
Hot Chili Neutral 00:16:06
  • Craig said he's "not the biggest fan" of Hot Chili's core copper project — a porphyry deposit stuck in a years-long drill/study loop, expensive and slow to advance, with a recent post-tax IRR of only ~19%, which he called underwhelming.
  • Flagged the La Verde deposit as the part likely to prove up into a genuinely strong resource over the next few years.
  • Said the more interesting part of the business isn't the copper project itself but a separate, more advanced regional asset that stands as a "really viable and solid business" on its own, even ignoring the flagship project.
  • Overall view: strategic appeal from scale and surrounding land holdings, but likely needs a partner or acquirer to fund development given the size and cost.
Hammer Metals Bullish 00:33:50
  • Craig framed Hammer's move to acquire surrounding exploration ground (rather than spending restart capital on a takeover) as a smart, low-cash-cost use of capital.
  • The deal gives Hammer a stake in CNB plus land wrapped around CNB's Trecolano and Mount Hope deposits, along with tenements bordering TNC, BTM and LRV holdings in the same district.
  • Said the real value is the regional land position, not the Kalman deposit itself, which he called "pretty average at best" — around 165m at 1.96% copper-equivalent (0.46% Cu, with molybdenum/rhenium credits lifting the CuEq grade).
  • Framed this as a classic district-scale consolidation play — Hammer picking up ground with future discovery/M&A optionality around a broader Queensland copper-gold endowment.
BWN Bullish 00:51:45
  • Craig called BWN's latest operational update "really, really nice," coming after a guidance downgrade and a steep sell-off a few months earlier.
  • Management responded to that sell-off by buying large parcels of shares on-market, which Craig reads as a genuine confidence signal.
  • Described the underlying business as high quality, stable and in demand, with exposure to offshore oil & gas support work (vessels/tugs) that should benefit from rising activity.
  • Said debt remains manageable provided operational performance keeps improving.
FLG Neutral 00:02:05
  • Brief chat-driven check-in on FLG; the share price has kept drifting lower after bouncing around 15-16c last month.
  • Craig's view: the pullback just sets up a better entry point rather than being a red flag.

Session Themes

  • Fundamental analysis means reading past headline announcements to understand who benefits and why — ownership structure, financing motives, and incentives matter more than the announcement title.
  • Concentrated ownership combined with control of both equity and debt is a recurring red flag in ASX resource takeovers (CAY, with Wyloo/Hastings and AIS cited as reference cases).
  • Regional land consolidation (Hammer Metals/CNB/Hot Chili district) can be worth more than the flagship deposit itself.
  • Insider buying after a sell-off (BWN) is read as a genuine confidence signal when paired with stable underlying fundamentals.
  • Resource size alone doesn't create value — metallurgy, processing complexity and commodity price assumptions determine whether a deposit is actually economic.

  • Cash position and free-carry/JV-funded exploration structures (CVN, GRL) valued as ways to gain exposure or optionality without full capital risk — but timing/catalyst distance still matters for near-term conviction
  • Consistent reminder that headline resource size means little without grade, metallurgy, infrastructure and capex context (AGY's lower grade raising its capital intensity)
  • General theme: don't dismiss a name permanently after a past disappointment (AGY), but require fresh evidence (DFS) before re-engaging

  • Recommended building watchlists and letting a company execute across multiple announcements before committing capital, rather than reacting to a single release
  • Consistent emphasis on resource confidence classification (measured/indicated/inferred) and project economics (IRR, capex, payback, mine life) over headline resource size

  • In-situ recovery (ISR) technology flagged as an emerging extraction method spreading beyond uranium into copper and rare earths — potential early-mover advantage for companies that can commercialise it, but execution risk remains high since the technology is still relatively immature commercially.
  • Craig reiterated that production capacity alone has little value unless there's enough resource to keep processing infrastructure running efficiently over time.
  • Noted that algorithmic trading increasingly reinforces the same support/resistance/momentum levels discretionary traders already watch, making classical technical levels more self-fulfilling.
  • Capital raisings flagged as potentially transformative signals — who participates, at what price, and how funds are deployed all say something about management confidence and project quality.

Session Themes

  • All four major ASX gold producers "smacked down" at least 5% (some more) this morning.
  • Craig linked the weakness to geopolitical volatility — military conflict headlines followed by a ceasefire announcement spiked and then dumped oil, adding uncertainty across commodities generally.
  • Gold itself had been attempting a rally recently, but that rally looks like it may be stalling.
  • Reminder that even a strong long-term commodity theme can produce sharp short-term drawdowns in a commodity-heavy portfolio.
OSL Bullish 00:06:02
  • OncoSil (OSL): clinical trial results due in June were released today; stock up ~20% on the day, on top of a recent 200%+ move around an earlier product approval.
  • Trial combined OncoSil's cancer-treatment device with folfirinox chemotherapy; result showed an extra ~18 months of median survival for patients — a very strong outcome.
  • Two co-primary endpoints (safety/tolerability and local disease control) were both met.
  • Craig's process note: don't pile in immediately on a good biotech readout — there's a time lag while the company meets with the FDA/TGA and designs/gets approval for the next trial. Keep it on the radar and watch for timelines to emerge over the next month or two.
LKO Neutral 00:09:07
  • Oil/gas name Craig flagged last week after an unexplained price pump; today's update fits the theory he had at the time.
  • Company is now re-testing flow rates on wells that previously had issues and were closed in, using new equipment and a different testing approach; pressure has been building and testing is now underway.
  • "So far, things are on track," but Craig stresses oil & gas timelines run in months, not days/weeks (production/pressure/gas testing and flow rates take a month or two to read), so it's still early to draw conclusions.
WCE Bearish 00:12:29
  • Announcement headline read positively — silver mineralisation extends 70m beyond the maiden resource and remains open — but the share price fell as much as ~12% (10% at one stage) on the day.
  • The issue was grade, not presence of silver: new extension results came in at 25g/t, 31g/t and 33g/t silver, versus the existing resource grade of 617g/t silver.
  • WCE's whole thesis has been built on being a high-grade silver story; these new low-grade intercepts raised concern that the high-grade core may be closing off and that future resource growth could dilute overall project grade/economics.
  • Craig's teaching point (his "FUN 101" framework): never judge an announcement by the headline alone — always check grade quality, economic significance and how it fits the existing resource before reacting.
PHO Bullish 00:20:14
  • Consistent, incremental growth in PHO's resource inventory across multiple areas already being considered in mine planning.
  • Craig thinks this could reach a "step change" moment — adding more mineable inventory changes project scale, economics (economies of scale) and potential mill throughput.
  • Watching for BFS progress and further resource additions as the next leg of the story.
CBY (Carnaby) Bullish 00:29:13
  • New drilling confirmed both the true width and grade of the "Mini Boom" copper mineralisation — angled holes (following an earlier hole drilled straight down the deposit) now suggest a true width of roughly 15-20m.
  • Market sold the stock down on the news despite this being a genuine confirmation/de-risking result — Craig was clearly frustrated with the reaction and remains bullish on the underlying resource story.
  • On top of the drilling news, Carnaby also completed a $7m placement.
ZNC Neutral 00:42:17
  • Subject of a scrip-for-scrip takeover offer from Forrestania Resources (FRS): 1 FRS share for every 4.3 ZNC shares, implying ~13.2c per ZNC share and roughly a 50% premium to the 10-day VWAP.
  • Share price only traded up to ~10.5c, short of the implied offer value and below where Craig expected it to settle (11.5-12c) — a bit surprising to him.
  • No independent expert report included in the transaction documents; Craig's read is that's because the deal terms are obviously favourable enough that one wasn't considered necessary.
  • Watch for formal takeover documentation and shareholder vote progress.
FRS Neutral 00:40:37
  • Acquirer in the ZNC scrip-for-scrip takeover (see ZNC above); ZNC shareholders who don't sell on-market will end up holding FRS shares.
  • No standalone view given on FRS itself this session — purely covered in the context of the ZNC deal terms.

Session Themes

  • "Context is king": the core lesson of the session — never judge an announcement by its headline; check grade quality, project stage, economic significance and how new information fits the existing resource/market expectations (WCE was the textbook example).
  • Understand where a company sits in its development lifecycle (discovery, resource growth, economic studies, development, production) — different stages attract different investors and valuation drivers.
  • Biotech results are only one step in a longer process — positive endpoints still require regulatory pathway clarity, further trials, and commercialisation timelines before a re-rate is "safe" to chase.
  • Oil & gas exploration runs on much longer timeframes than metals exploration — expect months of lag between announcements (spud, testing, flow rates) and meaningful outcomes.
  • Incremental resource inventory growth (PHO) can eventually produce a step change in project economics — worth tracking even when individual updates look small.
  • Takeover mechanics: scrip-for-scrip terms, VWAP-based premiums, and when an independent expert report is (or isn't) required are useful things to understand when a portfolio holding receives a bid.
  • Psychological/process theme: avoid "headline investing" — a positive-sounding headline doesn't guarantee a positive outcome; be patient through multi-stage development cycles rather than expecting fast payoffs.

  • Market cap currently ~$55m; Craig expects it to fall substantially once the distributions/spin-out complete since most of the current value was built on the royalty and RXL holding
  • Questioned the decision to return nearly all the capital rather than retaining some to fund a new acquisition
SRJ Neutral 00:02:52
  • Share price ran up significantly into the formal announcement confirming SpaceX as the contract partner — the market had largely identified SpaceX as the likely customer ahead of confirmation
  • Once confirmed, much of the anticipated value was already reflected in the price, and the stock sold off — a textbook case of selling into a fully priced catalyst
  • Key lesson: understanding when information becomes effectively known to the market matters more than the official announcement itself
  • Watchlist: post-announcement market reaction, future commercial developments from the relationship, potential regulatory scrutiny around disclosure timing
CAS Neutral 00:13:00
  • Remains in an exploration-intensive phase with ongoing gold mineralisation discoveries and a strong cash position supporting further drilling
  • Primary challenge is converting scattered mineralisation into a clearly defined, large-scale deposit
  • Discussion covered shear-zone interpretation, geological targeting, aircore drilling to identify anomalies, and follow-up RC drilling to build confidence
  • Generating encouraging geological evidence but has not yet demonstrated the scale needed for a major re-rating
GRL Neutral 00:06:05
  • Large shareholders High Fidelity Capital and Geoscan Consulting moved to remove all 3 existing directors, citing years of dissatisfaction with management given the low share price/valuation and lack of progress on a decent asset (Lewis Ponds)
  • Legal counsel has raised questions around the validity of the removal notice; outcome uncertain — Craig expects more clarity over the next 3-4 months and says this could decide the company's future direction/strategy
  • Separately, GRL plans to spin out its clay-hosted rare earth project (one of the larger such projects in Australia) into a new company, potentially by year-end, with GRL holders receiving shares in the new entity
  • Rationale for the spin-out: GRL is a small company that has made minimal progress on both Lewis Ponds and the rare earth project simultaneously — hard to fund both, so separating them makes sense

Session Themes

  • Markets frequently price in major announcements ahead of official confirmation (SRJ/SpaceX) — understanding when information becomes widely anticipated matters more than the announcement itself
  • Resource development is sequential (exploration → discovery → resource definition → feasibility → funding → development → production); each stage reduces risk and creates value, and not all exploration success is equal until it builds towards a coherent, scaled deposit model
  • Strategic infrastructure acquisitions (Sunshine Metals' Mount Moss purchase) can sometimes create more value than additional exploration success by shortening the path to production
  • When a company's market cap is substantially built on a single royalty/shareholding rather than its own operating assets (VMC), question what's left to justify the valuation once that asset is monetised and distributed
  • Activist shareholder actions and corporate restructures (GRL's director-removal push and rare earth spin-out) can be genuine catalysts for a company's future direction — worth monitoring even while the outcome remains uncertain

Session Themes

FA in Practice: Meet Stephen Biggins, Executive Chairman of SLB (Stelar Metals)

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Friday 29 May 2026
Bullish Setups: SLB
Bearish Setups: None
Neutral / Watching: None
SLB (Stelar Metals) Bullish 00:00:12
  • Stephen Biggins (Executive Chairman) is the same team that took Core Lithium from discovery through to production in the Northern Territory — Craig frames this as "Aussie mining royalty" returning to the same region to try to repeat that outcome, making management's track record a central part of the thesis.
  • SLB has just acquired the Hill of Leaders tungsten project (NT) after ~15 months of assessing and rejecting other opportunities before committing — Biggins was explicit that patience during selection, then immediate urgency once committed (field programs and drilling prep started before the deal was even formally announced), is deliberate strategy.
  • Acquisition criteria walked through on-air: right commodity (tungsten), right jurisdiction (NT, where management has deep operational/regulatory relationships from Core Lithium), right counterparties (people management knows and trusts), a deal structure that minimises dilution, and sufficient geological scale potential to justify the team's time and capital.
  • Deal structure is staged, with further consideration to the vendor tied to (1) significant drilling results and (2) delivery of a JORC tungsten resource — with an option to settle in cash later, when SLB expects re-rated shares to make that cheaper for shareholders than paying in scrip now.
  • Company is currently very tightly capitalised — enterprise value cited on the call at roughly $6-7M — which management explicitly frames as giving shareholders significant leverage to exploration success given the size of the opportunity.
  • Tungsten market thesis: prices have risen sharply over the past ~18 months on tightening Chinese export controls and growing Western/defence demand for a non-Chinese supply chain (tungsten's extreme hardness, density and highest melting point of any metal make it a genuine strategic/defence material) — Biggins compared the setup to the early stages of prior commodity cycles.
  • Technical detail: typical global cutoff grade for tungsten resources is ~0.05% WO3, with average global deposit grades around 0.15-0.2% WO3 (cited comparable NT-region deposits Hatchers Creek and Morley Hill in that range); higher-grade tungsten deposits exist elsewhere but are typically very small (a few metres wide, only 1-2Mt) — management's pitch for Hill of Leaders is combining known high-grade surface mineralisation with genuine scale potential, rather than the usual grade/scale trade-off.
  • Historical drilling at the project was shallow (averaging ~10m depth) and limited, leaving it largely underexplored by modern standards; the exploration hypothesis being tested is that shallow veins may merge into thicker, larger mineralised systems at depth (using geological models drawn from major Chinese tungsten systems).
  • Nearby comparable/peer project TGN was referenced directly as an example of the market re-rating a similar-geology tungsten story over the past year.
  • Program: Phase 1 (already underway) is surface mapping, rock-chip sampling and drill-target refinement; Phase 2 is RC (and potentially diamond) drilling testing depth extension, targeted to start in July once approvals (expected June) are through. If results support it, management is targeting a maiden resource as early as H1 2027.
  • Biggins emphasised his own personal shareholding and direct financial exposure to the company's outcome as an alignment signal for the audience.

Session Themes

  • Live case study in Craig's stated acquisition-evaluation framework: commodity selection, jurisdiction, partner/counterparty quality, deal structure and geological scale potential all treated as separate, explicit checkboxes rather than a single "good story" judgement.
  • Reinforces that management's previous success (discovering and developing a project in the same jurisdiction before) is treated as a standalone, significant part of the investment case — not just the project's geology in isolation.
  • Execution speed after acquisition (immediate field programs vs. sitting on the deal) is highlighted as a specific positive signal distinct from the underlying asset quality, since it creates continuous news flow and compounds value-creation opportunities.
  • Patience during due diligence (15 months, many rejected opportunities) paired with urgency once committed is presented as the correct temperament for resource-sector deal-making, rather than a contradiction.
  • Tight capital structure plus a staged, vendor-aligned deal structure is framed as a deliberate way to maximise shareholder leverage to exploration success while minimising unnecessary dilution.

FPH Bullish 00:01:04
  • Fisher & Paykel Healthcare's results came through well, providing rare strength in a healthcare sector that has otherwise seen little.

But the project starts at only 150,000 tpa (ramping from ~4,000-8,000 t/month), targeting that rate around Q1 2027 at the earliest, and needs a further ~$5M capex before it can even step up toward the 300,000 tpa / $25M EBITDA case.

  • Craig had predicted this raise days earlier and calls the project now "over the line" — after 20-odd years, they can finally hit go — but stresses the financing came at a "massive" dilution cost, and flagged a further cap raise and an eventual share consolidation as likely down the track.

GT1 Bullish 00:32:58
  • Lithium sits only 5th/6th on Craig's preferred-commodity list, but he still wants exposure, and GT1 (a Canada-based hard-rock lithium developer with two defined deposits — Seymour and Root) is his preferred way to play it.
  • Just recapitalised via an ~$11M raise (at a 30-40% discount) that fully funds the company through to an expected Final Investment Decision around March 2027; permitting is largely done (only native title equivalent and mine closure plan remain).
  • DFS due around September; the prior PEA (scoping study) showed an after-tax NPV of US$251M and 33% IRR.

  • Valuation concern: ~$250M market cap against only a 250koz gold inventory — compared unfavourably to peers ODY (~400koz+ for ~$50M) and Flagship (~2Moz for ~$80M), with BKB (gold+silver) sitting at ~$130M.

Session Themes

  • Core FA-scanning framework repeated throughout: identify the catalyst behind a price move, assess whether it materially changes company value (vs. temporary excitement), and check whether the operational scale can actually support the valuation being priced in.
  • "TA is responding to FA" — repeatedly used to explain why technical breakouts were occurring (GNM's acquisition, ARU's financing resolution, AGR's phosphate news), reinforcing that fundamentals lead and technicals confirm/time the move.
  • Recurring valuation-context discipline: market cap vs. resource ounces (TOR vs. ODY/Flagship/BKB), market cap vs. NPV (GT1), and EBITDA-at-full-run-rate vs. actual near-term production (AGR) were all used to separate thematic excitement from what the numbers currently support.
  • Dilution and financing structure were treated as central to the investment case, not a footnote — ARU's raise unlocked the project but at real shareholder cost, while GT1's fully-funded status through to FID was framed as a genuine de-risking positive.
  • Healthcare flagged as an emerging area for defensive capital rotation, but only into names with already-proven earnings delivery (FPH), not speculative turnaround stories.

  • Chart discussion touched on a hypothetical/illustrative pullback scenario (~$7 level referenced) to frame just how large the past re-rate has been relative to a possible drawdown.

Session Themes

  • Core format theme: Craig identifies where improving fundamentals are emerging before the broader market has re-rated a stock, then Jamie overlays technical structure (Fibonacci retracements, support/resistance flips, Elliott Wave, OBV/momentum) to time entries and confirm or challenge the fundamental read.
  • Gold sector: elevated prices are flattering margins across the board, but the group repeatedly warned against complacency — capital discipline (debt paydown vs. dividends) now will determine which producers avoid a "debt wall" when the next cycle turns.
  • Copper sector: financing structure is treated as a key differentiator — companies with offtake/funding already locked in (RTG via Glencore) were framed as materially de-risked versus peers still seeking capital.
  • Repeated emphasis on probabilistic thinking in the technical work — no wave count or fib level is treated as certain; the group stressed staying adaptable as price action evolves rather than marrying a single prediction.
  • Broader lesson: market sentiment often lags improving fundamentals, and the "old story" still being priced by the market can be the source of asymmetric opportunity once technicals begin to stabilise alongside improving fundamentals.

FAQ Fridays

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Friday 22 May 2026
Bullish Setups: EDE, RAC, ALV
Bearish Setups: LKE, 29M
Neutral / Watching: GHY, AVE
GHY Neutral 00:11:24
  • Helium/hydrogen wells (gold hydrogen) — Craig stresses the company has no booked resource or reserve estimate at all yet; nothing has been flow-tested to confirm actual production rates or commercial viability.
  • Flow testing is imminent (mobilising within about a week), with results expected by end of June, potentially into July if delayed — this is the key upcoming catalyst, analogous to a maiden MRE for a resource company.
  • Craig's specific criticism: the company's announcements (including plans for "commercial scale pilot plants" and various development pathways) are written as though outcomes are close to a given, when in reality everything is still hypothetical until flow test results land — recommends treating all current announcements as blue-sky planning, not confirmed progress.
  • Domestic angle is genuinely attractive if it works: Australia is a 100% net importer of helium, and Craig likes the idea of prioritising a fast-start helium project ahead of hydrogen given constrained global helium supply (partly Middle East-related).
  • Even a successful flow test doesn't mean rapid commercialisation — significant further engineering, studies and time would still follow before any production.
LKE Bearish 00:17:37
  • Lithium brine project — Craig's core criticism is grade: significantly below what's generally considered a commercially viable brine grade (roughly two-thirds below the accepted threshold), which is exactly the kind of marginal deposit Direct Lithium Extraction (DLE) technology is being developed to try to rescue.
  • Ownership structure is a specific concern: institutional ownership is under 1% of the register despite the company's age and stage (post-DFS, seeking offtakes/financing) — retail holds ~90%, making the stock unusually susceptible to sentiment-driven swings rather than being anchored by patient, sticky capital.
  • Cash position (~$15.3M) covers only ~4-6 months at current spend; the company also holds a ~$46M ATM facility, but Craig cautions this shouldn't be counted as guaranteed runway since it depends on market conditions and dilutes via share issuance whenever drawn.
  • DFS metrics are weak and were deliberately incomplete in the announcement: post-tax NPV (~US$1B) is less than the CapEx required (~US$1.16B), and post-tax IRR is only ~19.7% — Craig flags the omission of post-tax figures from the main announcement (despite being required for a DFS) as a red flag suggesting management knew the numbers looked poor pre-tax already.
  • Pursuing full downstream lithium carbonate production (not just concentrate/chloride) adds significant technical/cost complexity; the DLE technology involved has not yet been used at commercial scale anywhere in the world, meaning first-of-a-kind scale-up risk on top of the marginal underlying economics.
  • Craig's explicit conclusion: "nothing in this at all gives me any hope or confidence or desire to ever be invested in LKE" — contrasts it with lithium names that actually made it to production (PLS, Galan, Liontown, CXO) as the small minority of boom-era names that had genuine underlying quality.
EDE (Eden Innovations) Bullish 00:37:42
  • Carbon-nanotube-strengthened concrete technology (durability/strength advantage over standard concrete) — technology itself is not new (in testing/pilot use since ~2014-2015), but the company has become debt-free via convertible note conversion and a well-timed institutional placement (~$4M at a 41% premium to the 15-day VWAP).
  • Recent share price strength is attributed to two factors: the debt clearance (removing a long-standing overhang) and a new marketing push ("Eden Shield") repositioning the same core product for defence/critical-infrastructure applications — Craig is explicit this is a marketing repositioning of an existing product, not a new technology, but rates it as a smart way to access a market (and investor attention) the company wasn't previously part of.
  • A decade of durability field data (from long-running pilot programs, particularly in India and the US) is now sellable, which Craig sees as the underlying driver of increasing real sales/contract growth, separate from the recent share price momentum.
  • Financial reality check: still early-stage revenue (~$500k last quarter), not yet at breakeven, and will need to manage costs carefully as it scales into new contracts and markets.
RAC (Race Oncology) Bullish 00:45:11
  • Repurposing bisantrene, a drug originally approved in the 1980s for acute myeloid leukaemia, leveraging decades of pre-existing safety/efficacy data to skip years of early-stage work other biotechs would need to redo from scratch.
  • Two areas of interest: cardioprotective properties (protecting the heart from chemotherapy-related damage, which otherwise causes long-term/premature-death risk in cancer survivors) and standalone anti-cancer activity — the combination suggests potential for a drug that fights cancer while protecting the body from treatment side effects.
  • Currently running phase 1 trials only (safety-focused, not efficacy-proving) — the CPAC trial (cardioprotection + anticancer combined with another cancer drug) has just been cleared to progress into its dose-optimisation stage, the near-term catalyst to watch.
  • A reformulation (from RC110 to RC220) required re-running safety trials on the new formulation, which has been part of what's slowed the company's timeline.
  • Aspirational long-term goal is a phase 3 trial in acute myeloid leukaemia, but that is not yet active — Craig cautions members not to treat phase 3-related information as current.
  • Craig's view: normally phase 1 data isn't a major catalyst, but given the extensive pre-existing data on bisantrene, this phase 1 readout carries more weight than a typical phase 1 result would.
29M (29Metals) Bearish 00:51:39
  • Extended case study in cumulative operational risk: Capricorn Copper has been offline and flooded since early 2023 after extreme rainfall overwhelmed water mitigation systems — still years away from potential restart, requiring tailings storage facility approval/rebuild, a full restart feasibility study (not yet even started), then financing (more debt and/or dilutive equity) before construction could begin.
  • Meanwhile the second asset, Golden Grove, has suffered multiple seismic issues through 2025 disrupting zinc production (previously ~20% of revenue) — repeated guidance downgrades as fix timelines have slipped (from an expected April fix to now November/December).
  • Company already carries at least US$100M in debt and has done multiple capital raises; further raises are highly likely to fund both the tailings rebuild and any eventual Capricorn restart.
  • Craig's explicit framework: this level of company-specific, multi-year operational risk should disqualify a stock regardless of how attractive the broader commodity thematic (copper) is — draws direct parallels to taking on similar outsized risk in Boss Energy or Bellevue Gold during their own operational crises. Points out there are copper exposures available without this level of risk stacked on top of normal market risk.
  • Explicitly separates "the chart can still run" from "this is a good place to park capital" — acknowledges technical rallies can and do happen despite the unresolved fundamental risk.
AVE (Avecho) Neutral 01:02:28
  • CBD-based treatment targeting insomnia — described as the last credible remaining ASX candidate in this specific indication after every other company's CBD-insomnia trial has failed to show efficacy over placebo in a proper clinical setting.
  • Running what Craig believes is the largest trial of its kind conducted (at least in Australia) — has now enrolled enough patients to reach a phase 3 interim analysis (a go/no-go checkpoint), expected around end of June.
  • If the interim analysis supports continuing, it would confirm safety and give an early (not final) read that the data is showing a genuine effect — a meaningful catalyst either way given every prior attempt in this space has failed.
  • Regulatory upside if proven: the TGA has reportedly indicated it would fast-track an over-the-counter pathway if genuine clinical data supporting CBD for insomnia is produced, given existing informal/anecdotal use.
  • Craig previously held and exited this stock when an earlier time-lag broke his investment thesis — treats the upcoming interim analysis as the reason to watch it again, while being clear it could just as easily fail like every prior attempt.
ALV Bullish 01:05:50
  • Small (~$8-9M market cap) VMS (volcanogenic massive sulphide) copper-equivalent resource company — VMS deposits typically occur in geological clusters and carry multiple co-located minerals (copper, silver, lead, zinc, sometimes gold), and having already-defined resource at this market cap size is described as rare.
  • A likely discovery at the Touro prospect needs more confirming drill results before being treated as confirmed — most results there so far are weaker than elsewhere on the project, which Craig attributes to VMS mineralisation typically sitting deeper than what's been drilled so far rather than the target being absent.
  • Standout feature: 70% of the register held by the top 20 holders, including a quality institutional/long-money holder (Lowell Resources Fund) — Craig calls this level of "sticky" institutional conviction at such an early, small-cap stage genuinely rare and a strong confidence signal.
  • No material change to the thesis since prior coverage — 20-30 additional exploration targets remain to be tested across the clustered VMS system; a modest premium-priced placement recently helped fund the current drilling run.

Session Themes

  • Explicit, detailed case study (29M) on why "extreme, stacked, multi-year operational risk" should disqualify a stock regardless of thematic appeal — directly generalised to Boss Energy and Bellevue Gold as other examples of taking on excessive company-specific risk within an otherwise-favoured sector.
  • Recurring emphasis on institutional ownership percentage as a proxy for share price stability/sentiment-resistance — low institutional ownership (LKE, under 1%) is treated as a specific vulnerability, while high-quality institutional presence at a small market cap (ALV) is treated as a rare, meaningful positive signal.
  • DFS/study disclosure scrutiny reapplied: flags a company omitting post-tax NPV/IRR figures from a DFS announcement as a deliberate readability trick to obscure weak numbers, since post-tax figures are a mandatory part of a completed DFS.
  • Distinguishes genuine technological/product change from marketing repositioning of an existing product (EDE's "Eden Shield" defence pivot) — values the commercial strategy while being explicit with members that the underlying product/technology hasn't changed.
  • General reminder that phase 1 trial data is not usually a major catalyst on its own, but treats extensive pre-existing historical data on a repurposed drug (RAC's bisantrene) as a reason a phase 1 readout can carry more weight than it normally would.

BAR Bullish 00:09:45

  • Craig's core rule reinforced here: never take a new position during ramp-up — take profits at first-ore/first-production excitement, hold only a small residual position, and only re-enter once ramp-up issues are demonstrably resolved (contrasted with Polymetals/PLY, whose ramp-up went smoothly and is used as the "good" comparison case).

  • Shanghai-based engineering group (a top-tier, globally experienced mining engineering firm) is both a strategic shareholder and the party conducting metallurgical test work, drilling and study work — a strong technical/financial backing signal for the project actually being built.
  • Key trigger for the day's share price move: sold 13 percentage points of its 23% Zenith stake for US$20M, banking ~A$50M cash while retaining a 9% Zenith holding (plus future dividend exposure) — funds infill, extensional and metallurgical drilling plus study work well into next year without needing a capital raise (the company has only raised capital three times in its history thanks to the Zenith cash flow).
  • Next catalyst: an updated resource/study expected in ~6 weeks (mid-year), with Craig expecting the resource to grow from ~1Moz toward the ~1.5Moz range over time.

Session Themes

  • Reinforces the "never take a new position during ramp-up" rule in unusual depth using LOT as the negative case study and Polymetals/PLY as the positive comparison — explicit playbook: take profits at first-production excitement, hold a small residual position, only re-enter once operational issues are demonstrably resolved.
  • Repeated scrutiny of market-cap-vs-NPV mismatches as a valuation red flag, applied at very different scales (BAR's ~$8M cap undervaluing its own assets on the low end; NXG's ~$10-11B cap exceeding its own project NPV on the high end) — shows the same discipline applies regardless of company size.
  • Distinguishes genuine institutional conviction (a raise sized at more than half a company's market cap) from routine capital raising, treating raise size relative to market cap as a signal independent of the discount/pricing terms.
  • Reinforces that visually obvious rock-chip grades are not a substitute for drill-confirmed resource data when assessing early-stage exploration excitement (KAR) — ties back to the broader framework (soil sampling, geophysics, structural targeting) needed to judge exploration credibility.
  • Cost-growth-outpacing-revenue-growth flagged as a specific red flag pattern (Elders) — an "improving" headline result that requires a large step-up in costs to achieve is treated with more suspicion than a flat result achieved efficiently.

FA in Practice: Meet Chairman of WWI (West Witts Mining)

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Friday 15 May 2026
Bullish Setups: WWI
Bearish Setups: None
Neutral / Watching: None
WWI (West Witts Mining) Bullish 00:00:00
  • Koala Shallows (Stage 1, South Africa, Witwatersrand Basin): first new underground gold mine in South Africa in 15 years — DFS-backed, 17-year mine life, produces just over 1Moz over that period at an all-in sustaining cost under US$1,200/oz, ~3g/t run-of-mine grade.
  • Extraordinary regional endowment: this single lease has historically produced 31.2Moz — roughly half of Kalgoorlie's Super Pit output — within a wider goldfield that has produced ~1.5B ounces total; Michael notes the deposit is exceptionally well-understood after 130+ years of regional mining, giving it an unusually high (~85%) conversion rate from inferred to measured/indicated resource.
  • DFS uses a conservative, stress-tested base-case gold price of US$2,850/oz (with sensitivity analysis and a measured-and-indicated-only scenario also run) — explicitly contrasted by both Michael and Craig against a separate company's recent bankable feasibility study built on a US$4,200/oz base case, which neither of them believe reflects what banks will actually underwrite (current bank consensus price cited at ~US$3,200/oz).
  • At the US$2,850 base case, post-tax NPV is ~US$500M; at a US$4,000 gold price, Michael estimates NPV would move to ~US$700-800M — substantial disclosed upside versus the current ~A$250M market cap Michael cites as the medium-term target valuation once at full run-rate.
  • Production ramp-up is deliberately slow and disclosed transparently: ~4koz in year 1 (largely incidental ore from decline development, not proper stoping), ~20koz in year 2, ramping to a 70koz/year steady-state run-rate by around September/October 2028 — Michael flags the company won't be giving meaningful quarterly production guidance until around March/April 2027, once ore is coming from proper stopes rather than development work.
  • Payback-period comparisons to open-pit projects are structurally misleading in WWI's favour being read as worse than they are: open pits typically show 18-24 months of pre-production stripping before generating any ore, while WWI has been producing incidental ore from day one of decline development, artificially lengthening its apparent payback period in like-for-like comparisons.
  • Underground method suits the ore body (steeply dipping 45°, ~1.4m wide reef) far better than open pit would (uneconomic strip ratio at depth); currently hand-held mining using a modern hydraulic (not compressed-air) power system at shallow (~50m) depth, with mechanised stoping trials planned within 6 months as mining reaches steeper sections.
  • Social licence: converted initial adversarial opposition from 7 property developers (who had encroached on the tenement) into signed cooperation deeds with 6 of the 7 — improved local safety/security as a side effect of formalised development, and secured mains power connection due in October 2026 (replacing diesel generators).
  • Project 200 (the next major catalyst): a scoping study — due mid-to-late June 2026 — assessing scaling steady-state production from 70koz/year to a targeted 200koz/year, drawing on the same 7.24Moz resource (constrained above the 400m level; more gold likely exists below). Requires resolving two big questions: processing (refurbish/take over one of three nearby existing plants vs. build new — refurbishment favoured for lower cost and avoiding fresh permitting) and deposition (backfilling old historic voids, or trucking to a new regional tailings facility being built by DRD Gold — avoids creating a new waste dump next to the community).
  • Separate, optionality-rich dual-commodity project (Bird Reef Central, ~5-6km strike, only ~3km drilled): two parallel reefs only ~15m apart — the Monarch Reef carries uranium (exploration target 12-16Mlb U3O8 at 300-550ppm), the White Reef carries gold (previously excluded from studies at 2g/t when that was considered uneconomic, now viable at current cutoff grades). Historically ignored as a combined opportunity because the two predecessor lease-holders each focused on only one commodity and left the other in the ground. WWI already holds two of the three required uranium permits/certifications; infill drilling (~US$1.5-2M, already funded from the January raise) is pending final bank drawdown conditions being locked in, with results expected late 2026/early 2027. Longer-term, Michael flags a streaming deal (stream the easily-marketed gold to fund extraction, retain the uranium) as a natural financing structure once cash flow allows — noting the project was previously "too small" for major streaming players like Orion/EMR at Koala Shallows' scale, an option that opens up as the balance sheet grows.
  • January 2026 capital raise context: opportunistically upsized from an initial ~$20M institutional target to $33.7M at 8c (Tribeca alone increased its allocation from $4M to $10M) — executed in a single weekend without a formal roadshow, ahead of a subsequent gold price pullback following Middle East conflict escalation. Retired an earlier bridging loan (Nabarro) taken out mid-2025. Received genuinely mixed shareholder feedback (some praised the timing, others felt it was unnecessarily dilutive/early) — Michael's framing: take institutional money when it's available at a reasonable price rather than risk being forced to raise later at a worse price if market conditions turn, drawing on his experience through the 1987 crash and GFC. Company is now fully funded through to Project 200-stage decisions; management states any future raise would be for a specific growth opportunity (e.g. funding Project 200 infrastructure or accelerating uranium), not to "keep the lights on."
  • CapEx for Koala Shallows Stage 1 ~US$100M — roughly half from bank debt, with the remainder from equity plus ramp-up revenue generation during construction.

Session Themes

  • Extended discussion of why feasibility-study gold price assumptions matter for financeability — reinforces (consistent with prior sessions) that banks stress-test at meaningfully lower prices (~$3,200) than some companies' published base cases, and that a measured-and-indicated-only sensitivity case is what lenders actually rely on.
  • Detailed real-world walkthrough of underground vs open-pit trade-offs (mine life, payback period comparability, capital intensity, mechanisation potential) as a general educational framework, not just WWI-specific commentary.
  • Extensive treatment of community/social-licence management as a genuine derisking factor for underground mines located near population centres — presented as a replicable case study rather than a one-off.
  • Direct, unusually candid management commentary on the reasoning behind a controversial capital raise (timing, sizing, why a small-cap can lose out on larger funding structures like streaming deals by deliberately keeping initial capex low) — useful context for how executives think about capital raise timing versus market feedback.

SNM Bullish 00:25:56

Craig explains that simply re-cutting the existing drill data at current gold prices — without any new drilling — will mechanically pull more ounces into an economic resource and grow the headline figure.

BMN (Bannerman Energy) Bullish 00:33:42

AS1 Bullish 00:46:17
  • Revisited from the prior week's extension drilling announcement (proving mineralisation outside the existing resource) — since then, the company closed a $60M capital raise against a ~$230M market cap, a healthy raise-to-market-cap ratio in Craig's view.
  • Used as a detailed visual teaching example of JORC resource-confidence categories: indicated resource (~300m zone, tightly spaced drill holes) versus inferred (~1,300m zone, much wider drill spacing) versus a further ~3.5km of strike with only scattered holes and insufficient data to classify at all.
  • Craig's expectation: with $60M now available to fund aggressive drilling, the current inferred zone should convert toward indicated and the wider 3.5km strike should start entering the inferred category over the next 1-2 years as drill spacing tightens.
  • Frames this as a case where reading the resource map correctly lets you anticipate where future drilling and resource growth will occur before the market prices it in.
PXX Bullish 00:52:04
  • Two-pronged story: (1) a staged joint venture with Northern Star at the Alaska Range project (Caribou Dome + Stellar), where Northern Star funds exploration and can earn up to 60-70% of the project for a relatively modest outlay, having already transferred committed cash; and (2) PXX's own 100%-owned Humboldt Range project, where recent maiden drilling returned encouraging early results.
  • Existing scoping study on the Northern Star JV ground shows strong metrics — ~US$223M capex for a 74% IRR and a short payback period — and Craig believes there's more copper in the surrounding area (SACLY, Jupiter) that hasn't even been drilled yet.
  • Near-10-year mine life already in the scoping study; Craig expects updated capex (higher) offset by higher copper prices when the study is refreshed.
  • Northern Star's biggest-ever exploration program on this JV ground is set to begin around June/July as weather conditions improve.
  • ~$50M market cap — Craig rates PXX's underlying copper resource as better than many peer copper juniors, with the added benefit of being backed and largely funded by a major (Northern Star holds ~14-15% of PXX directly, on top of the JV funding).
AXL Bullish 00:58:08
  • Rare earths project — notably rich in dysprosium and terbium (the higher-value, less commonly discussed heavy rare earths) alongside the more typical NdPr, with metallurgical test work looking strong so far.
  • Planning to use in-situ recovery (ISR) extraction — potentially very low-cost, highly scalable, and low environmental disturbance if proven, drawing a direct analogy to Alligator Energy's ISR approach for uranium and to comparable rare earth ISR operations in China and Malaysia.
  • Field trial to prove ISR works in practice expected to start within the next ~12 months — the key catalyst that would make the resource genuinely economic if successful.
  • Only ~$12M market cap despite a resource base Craig says is larger than several more highly-valued rare earth peers — flags this valuation gap as the reason to keep it on the radar, contingent on the ISR field trial succeeding.

Session Themes

  • Repeated use of "what gold/commodity price is baked into the current MRE" as a way to anticipate resource growth before new drilling even happens (SNM's $2,200 vs current ~$2,800 gold price cut-off) — a specific, repeatable technique Craig teaches for spotting undervalued resources.
  • Consistent expectation-management on production timelines — explicitly corrects market/community assumptions that TNC and other developers are closer to production than their actual PFS/DFS/FID timelines support.
  • Institutional/major-partner backing via staged JVs and funding deals (Northern Star/PXX, CNNC/BMN, Tribeca-style raises) continues to be treated as meaningful de-risking, particularly when it removes the need for debt or forces favourable offtake terms.
  • Distinguishes normal institutional profit-taking/portfolio rotation (a holder trimming a position) from disorderly dumping — reinforces not overreacting to routine holder sell-downs.
  • Detailed use of resource-confidence maps (measured/indicated/inferred, drill spacing) as a recurring visual teaching tool for anticipating where a company's next resource upgrades will come from (AS1 example).

  • Mineral Hill (Cobar) underground gold-silver-copper operation — just had its best-ever quarter (helped significantly by the silver price and higher silver output from the open pit) but still only made ~$300k profit; without the silver price tailwind it likely would have lost money again.
  • ~$75M market cap, ~$25M cash — now transitioning from open pit into underground mining, which resets risk (compares favourably-run open pit operations as "de-risked" versus underground ramp-up risk returning).
  • Transitioning ore requires shifting from the CIL (leach) circuit to the smaller flotation circuit for copper/gold — likely needs further plant capex, funded status unclear pending more detail.
  • Current mine life is only ~5-6 years; management is targeting 10+ years but hasn't proven it yet — Craig believes there's more there but it needs to be demonstrated, and a proven 10-year mine life would materially change the investment profile.
  • Craig's overall take: better-positioned than in past years (consistent plant operation, good trial recoveries on copper), but the underground transition plus potential plant capex genuinely raises the risk level right now — not a "get excited" moment yet.
VUL (Vulcan Energy) Bearish 00:26:07
  • Craig has never been a fan and remains skeptical — corrects the framing upfront: Vulcan is not yet a lithium producer (construction only just started; possible production isn't until 2028).
  • ~€2.2B financing secured for phase 1 — more than the project's own post-tax NPV of ~€1.15B, which Craig calls "strange and not normally something you want to see."
  • Post-tax IRR of just 13% — a poor number in isolation; Craig notes projects with metrics this weak typically only proceed at very large scale, where the appeal shifts to long mine life/production volume rather than strong returns.
  • Additional execution risk from going downstream into lithium chemicals (hydroxide/carbonate) — a genuinely difficult, capital-intensive step Craig compares to IGO's Kwinana refinery still sitting at only ~51% of nameplate capacity three years in.
  • One differentiator in Vulcan's favour: parts of its technology/business model are designed to be licensed or replicated elsewhere, a repeatable-scale angle other lithium brine projects don't have.
  • Craig's bottom line: financially covered for now, genuinely well-executed fundraising, but the underlying project economics have never impressed him — flags a likely 3-6 month timeline slippage as a standard buffer to apply.
ARU (Arafura Rare Earths) Bearish 00:35:14
  • Addressed directly why big-name backers (Gina Rinehart, government funding) shouldn't be read as a bullish signal for retail shareholders: Craig argues these investors have essentially zero alignment with ordinary shareholders' timeframes, dilution tolerance, or return requirements — they can absorb decades-long payback horizons that retail investors can't, and their involvement mainly just draws more eyes (and can pump the stock) rather than reflecting a shared investment thesis. Draws on the historical example of Twiggy Forrest/Gina Rinehart/Chris Ellis blocking-stake plays in lithium that damaged rather than helped those projects.
  • ~25 years in development — Craig's standing concerns (timeframes, funding complexity, weak return metrics) are unchanged. CapEx guidance has moved around significantly (~$1.2B → ~$1.9B → ~$1.6B US across different updates).
  • 66% of offtake agreements signed; closing the remaining offtakes (particularly in Europe) is what triggers the rest of the funding needed to reach FID, expected around mid-year.
  • Project economics are "robust" (i.e., adequate, not outstanding) rather than strong — sub-20% IRR, and when the large headline NPV/free cash flow figures are averaged across the 38-year mine life, annual free cash flow is much less impressive than the big top-line numbers suggest.
  • Craig's explicit conclusion: doesn't fit his investment or trading strategy given the risk/time-lag versus the financial metrics — but he does see it as "a fantastic trading stock" given its volatility and headline-driven moves.
EUR (European Lithium) Neutral 00:45:31
  • Update on the previously covered Critical Metals Corp (CRML) takeover — an exclusivity period extension was just announced, meaning the deal didn't proceed to the original expected timeline.
  • Craig's guidance for existing holders: unless you specifically want to hold CRML shares post-merger, take profits now — the premium is already reflected in the price and the company has been dormant for years waiting for this moment.
  • Not a red flag per se (the companies are closely linked and a completed deal is still expected), but the extension itself is a reason for some caution — deals can still fall through, and any wobble could cost latecomers the extra 5-10% premium.
  • Craig would not enter fresh at this stage — limited further upside for new money versus real (if modest) binding risk.
RXL (Rox Resources) Neutral 00:47:44
  • Final Investment Decision made and fully funded (~$300M+ in debt approved plus equity) — construction genuinely underway, 2Moz resource / 674koz reserve, targeting ~117koz/year average production.
  • Mine life is only ~7 years currently — shorter than the ~10-year threshold debt financiers typically prefer; Craig was somewhat surprised the debt funding was approved given this, and expects the company is banking on converting more of the resource into reserves over time to extend it.
  • Valuation comparison: at ~$550M market cap, Rox trades at a large premium to comparable emerging gold producer Theta Gold Mines (TGM, ~$200M) despite TGM having a larger resource (6Moz vs 2Moz), similar financial metrics, and lower construction costs — some premium is justified by Rox's lower jurisdictional risk (vs South Africa), but Craig thinks the gap is larger than that alone explains.
  • Craig's view: $550M already prices in a high level of execution success and strong production ramp-up — a fair amount of good news is already baked into the valuation, so the bar for further re-rating is high.
WCE Neutral 00:53:28
  • First-ever maiden mineral resource estimate released: 2.8Moz silver — smaller than the market was expecting, and the share price sold off on the news.
  • High overall grade (617g/t silver) is genuinely excellent, but there's a large grade disparity between the indicated (137g/t) and inferred (1,331g/t) portions of the resource — Craig flags this gap as something the company will need to explain and close over time, and something he'd want to understand via the deposit maps before holding.
  • Puts the resource size in context: 2.8Moz silver converts to roughly a 40,000oz gold-equivalent resource — genuinely small in absolute terms, not a company-making deposit on its own.
  • Craig's framing: this project was never meant to be a large bulk-tonnage operation — the model (comparable to Elizabeth Hill) is a small, very high-grade, highly profitable operation, so investors expecting a large resource fundamentally misunderstood the project type; maintaining grade continuity in future updates matters more than growing tonnage.
  • Watch the relationship with the nearby Radio Hill processing plant (whose owners also hold an interest in WCE's tenements) — a future toll-processing agreement between the two is a plausible medium-term (3-5 year) development.

Session Themes

  • A recurring theme across nearly every question this session: separating "who is backing/associated with a stock" (Gina Rinehart on ARU, Tribeca on AUZ, big MOU partners on SOP-style news) from genuine alignment with retail shareholder interests — Craig explicitly warns against treating big-name involvement as a fundamental green light on its own.
  • Consistent skepticism toward large-scale projects with big headline NPV/funding numbers but weak underlying return metrics (IRR, free cash flow per year) — applied to both VUL and ARU as the same pattern: impressive scale, unimpressive returns once normalised.
  • Valuation-relative-to-peers comparisons used repeatedly as a check (RXL vs TGM) rather than assessing a company in isolation.
  • Reinforces that "reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction" is boilerplate JORC-code language required in every resource statement, not a meaningful company-specific claim — relevant both to exploration targets and to reading resource announcements generally.
  • Tribeca Investment Partners (and funds like LRT, LSX) flagged as generally constructive, long-horizon institutional holders whose involvement in a stock is a genuine positive signal, and whose public holdings lists are a legitimate source of investment ideas.

Market Mornings

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Tuesday 5 May 2026
Bullish Setups: RRL, VAU, SOP, KNI, AS1, RHT, VCX, AGE, PGO, GBR

AS1 Bullish 00:25:24

VCX (Vicinity Centres) Bullish 00:42:34

AGE Bullish 00:51:32

Session Themes

  • Multiple examples this session of Craig explicitly separating "the market's reaction" from "the underlying signal" — MCA's brutal cap raise pricing versus genuinely improved operations, KEY's suspicious volume spike versus a company giving no real answers, AGE's deliberately lower-expectation step-out testing versus the strength it actually demonstrates.
  • Recurring disclosure-quality theme: contrasts companies that explain guidance changes and unusual trading clearly (RHT, Hot Chili, AGE) against those that withhold context (GenTrak's guidance downgrade without a prior figure, KEY's non-answer to an ASX query).
  • Institutional participation in a raise, especially before results are fully confirmed (AW1-style, and again with SOP's financing facilities and MCA's underwritten raise), continues to be treated as a meaningful vote of confidence signal distinct from the raise terms themselves.
  • Large-scale industry consolidation (RRL/VAU merger) discussed as a broader confidence signal for the sector's outlook on funding big capital projects, not just a stock-specific event.
  • Craig continues to flag share dilution timing explicitly as a factor to weigh against otherwise-positive deal structures (GBR's near-doubling of shares on issue within ~6 weeks).

Fundamental Analysis Scan with Craig Dickson

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Tuesday 5 May 2026
Bullish Setups: HAR, ODY, AW1, BB1, FG1
Bearish Setups: None
Neutral / Watching: ALA, SNX, LGM
HAR Bullish 00:04:05
  • First assay results from the initial drill campaign have come through — narrow but high-grade hits, validating the historical (non-JORC) resource estimate of ~300koz.

  • JORC-compliant mineral resource estimate expected mid-to-late May (Craig expects some slippage, pencils in "end of May" as a safer estimate) — should come in at least in line with, likely better than, the historic estimate given gold found outside the known areas.
  • Deep/extension drilling continuing through July should keep adding mineralisation outside the current resource.
  • Craig's view: resource likely grows from ~280-300koz toward 400-500koz over time, with a path to 1Moz+ possible if the company can keep funding drilling — "the FA just keeps getting better and better" on this one.
ODY (Odyssey) Bullish 00:08:38

  • Drill rigs currently turning; scoping study and an updated MRE (likely larger, given drilling outside the current resource has hit gold) both underway, though timeline is loose — Craig believes the company may be waiting on the JV mill agreement to go binding first so the scoping study can use real processing terms.

BB1 (BlinkLab) Bullish 00:44:00
  • $17M capital raise completed, funding the pivotal study now underway (first patients enrolled).
  • Prior pilot study (485 children, larger than the originally planned "couple hundred") returned 83.7% sensitivity / 84.7% specificity for autism (ASD) diagnosis via a 15-minute smartphone app tracking facial reactions and eye movements — on par with or better than traditional clinician diagnosis.
  • FDA-mandated threshold for the pivotal study is 65% sensitivity/specificity; all testing to date has been in the 80s, well clear of the bar.
  • FDA actually reduced the required pivotal study size (528 participants) after being satisfied with existing data — a positive regulatory signal.
  • App-based, at-home testing captures the full spectrum of cases (not just obvious/severe clinical presentations), which Craig frames as genuine stress-testing of the algorithm rather than cherry-picked easy cases.
  • Two FDA-approved competitor tools already exist (52%/71% and 19%/81% sensitivity/specificity pairs cited) — BlinkLab's results already beat both.
  • Key catalyst: pivotal study results expected toward the end of 2026 — that's the "go time" moment Craig is watching for.
LGM Neutral 00:49:02
  • Scoping study finally released (after a couple of weeks' delay); market sold the stock down ~15-20% on the day.
  • CapEx came in at ~$220M, above Craig's hoped-for $150-180M range — pushed the study's headline IRR/NPV figures lower than the market wanted, though $220M itself is a normal range for a gold-silver project of this type, not an outlier.
  • Study only incorporates ~373koz gold and ~9.9Moz silver (roughly half the ~700koz gold / ~20Moz+ silver in the full resource) over a 19-year mine life, and completely excludes copper, zinc and lead credits that exist in the resource — a deliberately conservative first-pass study, not a sign the deeper resource is being downgraded.
  • Metallurgical recoveries used (78% gold, low-80s% silver) are from early-stage test work and are expected to improve with further work ahead of the PFS.
  • Resource classification looks appropriate for this study stage: indicated resource covers the full payback period plus buffer (71% indicated in years 1-11), with inferred material only entering later in the 19-year mine life — standard and acceptable for a scoping study.
  • Craig's take: not a bad outcome despite the market reaction — new extensions and additional mineralised zones outside the current MRE are already being found, and the resource/study should both grow materially by the next study (PFS) in 6-9 months; expects a "time lag" while short-term holders exit before the next value-creation catalyst (new assays, updated study).
SNX Neutral 00:38:45
  • ~$30M market cap; Craig explicitly says he doesn't see the fundamental case others are excited about (a technical-analysis-driven follower had good TA-based trades on it, but Craig found nothing compelling in the FA).
  • Owns the old, historic Neapass mine (Nevada) — genuinely old workings, not a modern mine that can simply be "switched back on" despite some market chatter suggesting otherwise; current "trial mining" is small-scale metallurgical test work, not a real production restart.
  • Share price rally has mainly been driven by winning an exploration licence auction for the early-stage Safra copper-gold project in Saudi Arabia — Craig notes there's no defined resource and only very early rock-chip sampling has been done, and says plainly he doesn't understand what's driving the market's excitement about it.
  • Craig's explicit conclusion: "I don't get it" — flags this as a case where the share price move isn't well explained by the underlying fundamentals he can see, without a clear insider explanation either.
FG1 (Flinders Gold) Bullish 00:59:34
  • Silver assay results (from the Northwest Tasmania silver/zinc/lead/tungsten side of the portfolio) have come out and are described as "pretty good," though Craig was really waiting on Fire Tower results specifically.
  • Notable pivot in company messaging: after consistently promoting the Northeast Tasmania narrow-vein high-grade gold story (which Craig says he isn't keen on), the company suddenly shifted its latest presentation to heavily emphasise tungsten at Fire Tower — a project not previously given much airtime.
  • Craig likes Fire Tower on fundamentals (gold + tungsten, extensive historic drilling/assay data available for cheap re-assay rather than fresh drilling) and the Northwest silver projects more than the gold story the company has been pushing.
  • Reads the sudden tungsten focus as a signal something may be coming — possibly tied to an upcoming MRE update — and flags it as worth watching over the next month or two to see what's driving the change in emphasis.

Session Themes

  • Repeated defence of capital raises when the company clearly has a credible use for the funds (AW1, ODY) — Craig's litmus test is whether the raise size is actually sufficient to fund the stated work program, not whether a raise happened at all.
  • Distinguishing a "disappointing market reaction" from a "bad outcome": LGM's scoping study sell-off is explicitly reframed as conservative/early-stage rather than a red flag, using the resource-classification and CapEx detail to make the case.
  • Recurring emphasis on validating historic/legacy drill data with new results (HAR) as a capital-efficient way to build a JORC resource without re-drilling everything from scratch.
  • Corporate governance risk flagged directly and treated as reason for caution rather than speculation — ALA's sudden board clear-out is explicitly called out as a "stay cautious, don't assume business as usual" situation rather than spun positively or negatively.
  • Willingness to publicly say "I don't understand this rally" (SNX) rather than force a narrative onto a share price move that isn't well explained by visible fundamentals.
  • Noticing subtle shifts in company messaging/emphasis (FG1's pivot from gold to tungsten) as a signal worth investigating rather than ignoring.

FA in Practice: Meet James, the MD of AKA (Aureka)

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Friday 1 May 2026
Bullish Setups: AKA
Bearish Setups: None
Neutral / Watching: None
AKA (Aureka Gold) Bullish 00:00:00
  • James Gurry: 13 years at Credit Suisse/Deutsche Bank covering global metals & mining equities (Sydney/London), then took a board role turning around Flinders Mines (WA iron ore), which was sold to Fortescue for $250M — background is capital markets/corporate finance, not geology.
  • Joseph (technical lead): geologist since the 1990s, cut his teeth at the Fosterville Gold Mine during its early drill-out (before it became a world-class underground deposit), then 18 years abroad (Laos, Myanmar, 6 years with Eldorado Gold in China, Russia, Kyrgyzstan, and most recently Barrick's exploration manager for Tanzania/Côte d'Ivoire) — deliberately paired with James for complementary finance + technical skill sets, which Craig highlighted as a specific strength (Joseph credits Barrick's Mark Bristow for teaching him to explain geology simply without losing technical accuracy, to communicate with non-geologist stakeholders).
  • Flagship Irvine Gold Project sits in the Stawell Corridor, Victoria, directly adjacent to the 5Moz Stawell Gold Mine (Magdala deposit) — inferred resource of 304,000oz gold across the Resolution and Adventure lodes, plus an exploration target of 280,000-420,000oz.
  • Acquisition story: picked up 20 Victorian tenements (including the ~300koz Irvine deposit that once traded at a $150M market cap under predecessor Navarre Minerals) from an administrator for $525,000 after Navarre collapsed in 2023 following an unrelated failed Queensland mining venture — a classic distressed-asset pickup during a period when Victorian approvals and financing were both very difficult.
  • Drilling has moved from incremental step-outs (which took the share price from 10c to 19c on holes #48/#49 last year) to bigger "step-change" discovery-style holes drilled in the gap between Resolution and Adventure, underneath historic 1800s workings (Eaglehawk, John Bull, Native Youth) — aiming to prove up a much larger system, with management explicitly targeting a conceptual pathway to 1Moz and a $0.5-1B market cap.
  • A newly flown high-resolution drone magnetic survey (7km covering Resolution to Adventure) has revealed additional cross-cutting structures and flanking basalt targets not visible in the old regional dataset — management stresses the team came in with no preconceived interpretations from the previous company and is rebuilding the geological model from first principles.
  • Secondary project: St Arnaud/Comstock (65km strike, historical production of ~400koz at ~15g/t) — maiden resource of 56,500oz at 1.21g/t released May 2025, with an exploration target of 112,000-116,000oz; narrow, high-grade shear-hosted system (not suited to bulk open-pit) with silver credits up to 650g/t in some holes.
  • Comstock is being fast-tracked as a near-term, low-capex cash-flow project via a prospecting licence (minimal-disturbance, rehabilitation-style approach) and a toll-milling partnership with the nearby privately-owned Wedderburn mill (announced December) — explicitly designed to fund the Irvine exploration program without repeated equity raises; management targeting ~12 months to first production given Victoria has approved 4 new mining projects in the past year after a multi-year approvals drought.
  • Management frames the two projects as complementary rather than a scattergun portfolio: Comstock for near-term free cash flow, Irvine for the "10x" exploration upside — explicitly contrasted with juniors that stop-start between unrelated projects and lose market credibility as a result.
  • Stawell Gold Mine (privately owned, run for cash extraction under private equity ownership for 6 years per management) is reportedly short on mine life and needs more feed — management describes an active, friendly relationship with Stawell's people/stakeholders and sees a longer-term consolidation opportunity given the corridor was historically one integrated system (Kirkland Lake/Agnico Eagle).
  • Near-term catalysts flagged: infill drilling and scoping study results at Comstock (finalising licensing and mill agreement), and processed results from the new Irvine magnetic survey defining fresh step-out drill targets — both expected over the next 3-4 months.

Session Themes

  • A deep-dive illustration of Craig's management-quality framework in practice: explicitly draws out how complementary finance/geology skill sets and clear day-to-day communication between founders is a differentiator for junior resource companies.
  • Distressed-asset acquisition as a recurring theme — Craig and management both reference how weak financing conditions and corporate failure (Navarre's administration) can create deeply discounted entry points for well-positioned operators, drawing parallels to companies like Lovado and Iltani doing similar plays.
  • Capital discipline emphasised throughout: small team, no dedicated office, minimal overheads, and a specific strategy (Comstock cash flow funding Irvine exploration) designed to reduce reliance on repeated dilutive capital raises.
  • Craig repeatedly reinforces the value of a coherent, articulated company strategy (flagship exploration asset + funded near-term production asset) versus scattergun juniors that chase whichever project "lights up," arguing the latter destroys value when drilling programs stop and start.
  • Geological read-through from analog systems (Fosterville's evolution from small pits into a world-class underground mine) used to frame the long-term thesis for an underexplored regional gold corridor.

  • Post-tax NPV of ~US$860M (~A$1.4B) and IRR of 74% — well above Craig's preferred >35% IRR threshold.
  • Stress-tested at half the scandium price and still returns a profitable 32% IRR — passes Craig's "always stress-test the deposit" check.
  • Relatively low capex (~US$125M/~A$200M) against that NPV, and a 28-year mine life — comfortably above the 10-year threshold debt financiers typically require, which Craig says is often what holds back otherwise-popular projects (cited BML and early CXO as prior examples).

FDR Neutral 00:40:16

Craig is watching for the funding announcement over the next few months as the next major catalyst.
RKB Neutral 00:53:12
  • Tiny explorer (was ~$3-4M market cap) picked up what Craig called a "transformational" acquisition — an existing (non-JORC) resource of 320koz gold, alongside an $4M placement.

  • Deal structure is heavy on deferred consideration: $2.5M upfront (most of the $4M raise), $3M payable on first gold pour, another $3M a year after that, plus staged payments of $2M/$2M/$1.5M at 6/12/18 months payable in cash or shares.
