  • Bottom line: interesting asset, "terrible way to get it" — Craig is watching for a point where value and TA line up rather than treating this as a trade now.

Session Themes

  • Recurring theme of revisiting old "hype" names (lithium boom leftovers LIT and PL9/AZL) to separate genuine fundamental progress from lingering narrative — a direct example of Craig's "narrative vs reality" filter.
  • Strong emphasis on patience: waiting for post-announcement price consolidation before entering, rather than chasing initial spikes or trading halts on resumption.
  • Repeated use of stress-testing project economics (halving commodity price assumptions) and checking mine life against the ~10-year threshold that debt financiers require — used on AUZ as a worked example.
  • Deal-structure scrutiny as a core discipline: RKB's headline resource looked excellent, but reading through to the actual consideration structure (deferred cash + share tranches) revealed a heavy, fast-moving dilution risk that wasn't obvious from the resource number alone.
  • Craig reiterated his announcement-sourcing workflow (asx.com.au ticker search → full announcement history) as the standard way to verify a company's full disclosure record.
  • Format housekeeping: FAQ Fridays will run every second Friday going forward (next batch of questions opens this Friday, answered the following Friday); Craig is now also running a Tuesday midday Market Mornings session in addition to the Tuesday evening FA Scan.

Fundamental Analysis Showcase with Craig Dickson

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Tuesday 21 April 2026
Bullish Setups: QML, XPD, AGE
Bearish Setups: HFR
Neutral / Watching: NUF, HYT
HFR (Highfield Resources) Bearish 00:23:05
  • Craig used HFR as a "read the story before you jump in" case study: a big volume spike/candle got people excited on the chart, but the underlying FA is a genuine, ongoing downtrend for real reasons — "your TA cannot change the FA."
  • The potash project needed roughly A$1bn in funding and was close to fully financed through 2022-2024 (including a ~€320m raise and a ~US$300m cornerstone investment), but 2025 brought mining-permit issues and the mine is now stuck in court with no timeframe for resolution.
  • Major shareholder EMR Capital holds ~25% and is "buried" in the position; convertible notes came due that Highfield couldn't repay, forcing further leverage into convertible debt.
  • Craig's takeaway: don't chase an exciting-looking chart on a company in genuine trouble just because it "might jag" — he says that works roughly 10% of the time, and the other ~90% of the time "those ones are gonna suck."
NUF (Nufarm) Neutral 00:07:59
  • Came up while answering a viewer question on how to think about agricultural stocks through weather/El Niño cycles — Craig's rule of thumb: don't hold ag stocks long-term given weather volatility, unless the business is diversified away from direct crop exposure.
  • NUF currently has almost no direct grains/crops exposure (aside from crop protection products), plus seed technology and a possible future biofuels angle — but Craig flags "we'd certainly need to be careful with NUF," noting the company still has plenty of unresolved issues and its main near-term goal is cost reduction.
  • Contrasted against GrainCorp (direct grain exposure) and Elders (livestock/middleman business, minimal grain exposure) to illustrate the range of exposure types within the ag sector.
  • No trade call made here — used as an educational example of sector-exposure analysis rather than an active setup.
QML (QMines) Bullish 00:34:59
  • Craig's long-standing favourite in the copper space — strong project and location, resource consistently growing, good study results, progressing into a Definitive Feasibility Study with production possible in ~2-3 years.
  • Craig had flagged a cap raise as highly likely after the company paid off loans taken to accelerate its PFS, leaving little cash — that overhang has now eased with a Queensland government investment-arm funding announcement.
  • Government involvement should make other funders more comfortable lending at better rates; Craig now sees no cap raise near/medium-term if things play out as expected.
  • Craig's summary: "the FA gets even better for those guys" — existing holders should be happy with the outcome.
XPD Bullish 00:48:38
  • A catalyst play Craig likes because the drill target sat in an area with proven historic gold drill hits, rather than a speculative "hunch" — that skews the odds of a hit in the company's favour.
  • New assay results showed strong grades (27g/t and 3g/t in adjacent new holes vs 1.28g/t in an older nearby hole); geology didn't fully match between the old and new holes, so the company is re-checking its model rather than assuming the result is simply wrong.
  • Separately picked up a historic high-grade project (avg. 41g/t vs a 30g/t "bonanza" benchmark) hand-mined in the 1800s/early 1900s, acquired cheaply with no attached debt and minimal modern drilling — a pickup Craig says he "didn't see coming."
  • Company is in a trading halt for a capital raise to fund drilling across both projects — Craig approves of this approach ("how a company should cap raise"): raise once you have a strong asset, then fund proper drilling rather than dribbling out $1m at a time.
AGE (Alligator Energy) Bullish 00:45:10
  • Follow-up on a catalyst Craig had been tracking — the question was whether AGE could actually prove its in-situ leach (ISR) uranium extraction method, and the field-trial data (not lab/bench scale) confirms yes.
  • Trial is run directly at the deposit under real ground conditions (solution injected into the ground, contained by bedrock so it can't leach into the water table) — a genuine in-field process proof point, not a simulation.
  • More updated data expected over the next 2-4 weeks; so far "everything is looking really good... it looks like it is going to work."
  • Craig frames this as the type of story he likes best: fundamentals "just keep getting better and better" as each catalyst lands.
HYT (HyTerra) Neutral 00:20:25
  • US-based (Kansas) natural hydrogen explorer, discussed alongside its Australian-listed peer "Gold Hydrogen" as two comparable early-stage plays in the same emerging space.
  • Kansas location sits close to existing infrastructure, easing future commercialisation — but Craig notes that's still 1-2 years away, not imminent.
  • Near-term catalyst is flow/production testing on the first well to establish a commercial flow rate that could then support a financing push.
  • No trade stance taken — Craig is watching for the appraisal program to prove up before treating this as more than a watch item.

Session Themes

  • Macro overlay on agriculture-sector selection: weather-cycle risk (El Niño), direct vs. diversified/indirect exposure framing, and why ag stocks generally aren't suited to long-term holding.
  • "Read the story before you chase the chart" — HFR used as a cautionary case study showing a strong TA move doesn't override red-flag fundamentals (funding collapse, mine stuck in court, major holder "buried").
  • FA validation framed as an ongoing process, not a one-off scan — repeated emphasis on checking whether previously flagged catalysts (QML's funding overhang, AGE's ISR trial, XPD's drilling) actually played out as expected, rather than treating the initial thesis as confirmation.
  • Craig's exploration-quality filter: prefers drill targets in areas with proven historic hits over speculative "hunch" drilling, and likes capital raises that come after a company lands a strong asset and are sized to properly fund drilling rather than trickled out.
  • FA + TA + macro confluence highlighted as the strongest setup combination, with time horizon matched to the nature of the thesis (cyclical/catalyst-driven trade vs. genuine long-term hold).

  • Craig's standing view (reiterated, held for over a year): CNB's realistic end-game is a takeover by a major (most likely Glencore) given its position amid other Glencore-linked copper assets in the region, rather than growing into a standalone major producer.
CUE Neutral 00:52:41
  • Explained the mechanics behind Horizon's below-market takeover bid for Cue Energy (~13.5c market price vs ~14.3c implied offer value, a much smaller premium than typical): Horizon and Echelon (which already owns ~50% of Cue) have coordinated — Echelon on-sold Horizon a 19.9% stake specifically to support the bid, giving the two a combined ~50% voting bloc.
  • Underlying motivation: all four companies (Cue, Horizon, Echelon, CTP) are linked via the Mereenie/Marina gas field JV; Horizon and Echelon teaming up may let them challenge CTP's operatorship or take a larger share of that growing field's revenue over time.
  • Craig's take: the outcome hinges on how the remaining un-aligned block of Cue shares votes; the independent advisory committee's recommendation (due before the deal closes) will be a key signal. Considers the current bid a lowball offer and thinks Horizon could realistically raise it ~10%+ if the independent review pushes back.
  • Practical guidance given: sell on-market now if happy with a price near the implied offer and unwilling to gamble on a bump; otherwise hold through for the blended cash-plus-Horizon-scrip outcome if the deal proceeds as structured.

Session Themes

  • Extended teaching segment on Mineral Resource Estimates (MREs): initial "maiden" MREs are a known catalyst type; subsequent MRE revisions are not automatically positive — tonnage can rise while grade falls (or vice versa) — investors need to read prior drill results to judge the likely direction before playing an MRE update as a catalyst.
  • Extended teaching segment on metallurgical test work: consistently underrated by the market despite being one of the most important value drivers, especially for complex/rare-earth-adjacent commodities (gallium, niobium, germanium, titanium) versus simpler ones (gold, copper, lithium); cited recent Australian mineral sands failures (Strand line, Sheffield) as cautionary examples of processing risk destroying otherwise-promising projects.
  • Strong plug for the prior FA in Practice session with Stephen Biggins (Core Lithium founder), summarising his three-part framework for picking companies: commodity cycle positioning, people/management track record, and asset quality — explicitly applied this lens across today's picks (AXL, PTR, LGM).
  • Reiterated pattern-recognition trade setup: a name that "moonshotted" on a discovery, retraced most/all of the gain, and now has a fresh, genuine catalyst approaching (PTR, and to a lesser extent LGM) is one of Craig's core repeatable strategies.
  • Explained the hierarchy of feasibility studies (scoping study → PFS → DFS → BFS) and the distinction between a Mineral Resource Estimate and an Ore Reserve (much higher-confidence, bankable subset of the resource) in the context of CNB's PFS release.

Session Themes

  • Extended founder interview format: Stephen Biggins (founder of Core Lithium, non-exec roles at Winsome Resources/SLB/AUV) shared how he built CXO from exploration through to production, and his general framework for assessing projects and management.
  • Commodity-cycle positioning as the central theme: Stephen credits CXO's success largely to correctly reading the 2015-16 shift toward lithium/EV demand and positioning early, rather than any single discovery.
  • Emphasis on non-technical skills for company builders: an MBA and business/strategy training were described as equally important to geological skill in successfully running a resource company, since most technical people lack organisational/strategic experience.
  • Financing resilience during down-cycles: CXO survived the 2018-2020 lithium downturn by leaning on strategic/international relationships (battery makers, Jet Capital, Lithium Royalty Corp, Yahua) rather than retail equity markets, which had lost interest.
  • Repeated framework: "past performance of people is a strong indicator of future performance" — assess management track record as heavily as the asset itself.
  • Realistic development timelines reiterated across commodities: lithium/copper projects typically take 10-20 years door-to-door, rare earths potentially 20-30 years given Western processing/technology gaps versus China — a caution against expecting fast re-ratings in thematic sectors.
  • Risk-tiered framework for exploration vs. de-risked plays: early-stage "first drill hole" speculation can re-rate fast but has low odds of success, versus projects where geological/exploration risk has already been partly removed by prior drilling plus a credible team reinterpreting the data.

FA in Practice: Meet Andrew, the MD of AUV (Auravelle Metals)

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Friday 6 March 2026
Bullish Setups: AUV
Bearish Setups: None
Neutral / Watching: None
AUV Bullish 00:02:54
  • Formerly Seapa Resources (listed 1987); rebranded to Auroville Metals after Andrew (ex-analyst at Hartley's/JP Morgan, former MD of NTM Gold) brought in new South Australian and WA ground in Dec 2024/Feb 2025, alongside chairman Stephen Biggins (Core Lithium founder) and ~6%+ cornerstone holder Lowell Resource Fund.
  • Core thesis: Knuckle Hill/Tunkillia North sit on the same Yalbrinda shear zone (~3-5km wide, ~80-100km long) as Barton's Tunkillia deposit (1.6Moz, ~$280M market cap) just 15-20km away — same rocks, same structural "plumbing," not just proximity. Neighbouring Marmota's Aurora Tank find (~30km away, 900m mineralised strike, still open) triggered a 40% one-day share price jump and a ~$180M market cap, used as a direct comparable for re-rating potential.
  • Despite sitting on this 40km of shear-zone strike, the ground has seen very little modern drilling — most historical work was shallow 1990s Calcrete/soil sampling (Equinox, Dore), with almost no deep RC drilling; AUV is filling that gap.
  • First drill program at the Sheoak prospect (mid-2025, extended Aug/Nov) returned much better grades/widths than expected: ~200m of high-grade mineralisation within a ~600m anomalous zone still open north, south and at depth. Targeting built by stacking soil geochemistry (gold + silver anomalies), independent structural geology interpretation (dilational jogs/kinks in the shear) and multi-element analysis — a live demonstration of the "target stacking" method Craig teaches in the Fundamentals course.
  • 2026 plans: RC infill/extension drilling at Sheoak and Sheoak East, regional air-core discovery drilling across other stacked targets (Sheoak North, Mile, Sauna, Bimba West), first metallurgical test work at Sheoak (de-risking extraction, referencing Tunkillia's clean metallurgy as a positive read-through), a regional aeromagnetic survey, and first-pass soil sampling/air-core drilling at the Sky project (in the Woomera exclusion zone, ~12km from Marmota's Aurora Tank) from late March. ~7 drill programs planned for the year (up from 6 in the prior year); current ~$2M cash funds roughly the next two drill rounds.
  • Separate WA project (Crown, 40km from Kalgoorlie) is a lower-risk monetisation play: sits near multiple hungry processing plants (Black Cat's Majestic/Fingals, Horizon) with good road infrastructure, meaning even a modest ~50,000oz resource at 1.5-2g/t could be toll-milled profitably (~$3-4k/oz margin) without needing a company-making discovery — same air-core-then-RC targeting philosophy applied there too.
  • Valuation framing (from both Andrew and Craig): ~$10-12M market cap with an "outstanding risk/reward" skew — a move to even half of Marmota's ~$180M cap would be a ~9x return; downside at this small a cap is considered well protected versus a re-rated ~$25M+ cap, where a de-rate could be far more painful in percentage terms.
  • Governance/alignment signal: board (Biggins, Andrew, Lowell's John Forward, an investment banker chair) all hold meaningful equity, explicitly framed as aligning management incentives with shareholder outcomes.

Session Themes

  • Extended "founder walkthrough" format: AUV's MD explained the company's full targeting methodology live, explicitly framed by Craig as a model example of the "stacking data" approach taught in MtM's Fundamentals course (soils + structural geology + multi-element geochemistry all overlaid to generate drill targets).
  • Detailed teaching on drilling methods: air-core (cheap, shallow, first-pass screening to top-of-fresh-rock) versus RC (deeper, more expensive, used to follow up anomalies) — reiterated as critical context for judging whether a company's historical "lack of results" reflects a bad project or simply under-explored ground with only shallow drilling to date.
  • News flow as a junior explorer's "lifeblood": AUV's own share-price/volume chart was used to show turnover and price both stepped up materially once the company began actively drilling and communicating results, versus years of inactivity under the old Seapa identity.
  • Investing-hierarchy/cascading-capital framework: institutional capital flows to producers first, then developers, then advanced explorers, leaving early-stage juniors like AUV reliant on retail liquidity — explains why the company doesn't yet pitch to institutions despite already having Lowell on the register.
  • Macro backdrop discussion: gold's structural tailwinds (US dollar devaluation/debt, central bank buying, de-dollarisation) contrasted with local headwinds (higher interest rates reducing retail "punting" money), creating a possible disconnect between big-cap and small-cap gold stock performance.
  • Governance red flag reiterated: a junior board dominated by lawyers/accountants with no technical geologists is a warning sign — contrasted with AUV's mixed technical/finance/corporate board.

  • Read as a genuinely positive result for a mid-to-advanced-stage explorer specifically because of where the drilling was targeted, not just what it returned

Session Themes

  • Managing personal "mental load" (illustrated by Craig closing his own forex accounts to refocus on stock research) is framed as a legitimate, underrated part of investing discipline — reducing decision fatigue and distractions directly improves execution of your actual strategy
  • Recurring pre-earnings "TA wiggle then dump" pattern reiterated with fresh large-cap chart examples — always check recent trading updates/half-year results directly on the ASX announcements page before trusting a bullish setup into a known reporting date
  • Burying materially negative news (delayed guidance, cost overruns) inside a capital raise document rather than disclosing it separately is treated as a real credibility red flag, even when no actual disclosure rule is technically broken (LOT)
  • Distressed/turnaround situations (EM2) can become genuinely interesting when a credible larger partner completes real due diligence and progresses to legal documentation — but position sizing should reflect the speculative nature until final approvals land
  • Drill result context (infill vs step-out/extensional, position relative to the existing resource block model) is repeatedly flagged as more important to the market reaction than the raw assay grade alone (SLS)
  • Conservative management choosing to slow down and de-risk a resource (more infill drilling before a scoping study) is framed as a positive signal about capital discipline, not merely a disappointing delay (RR1)
  • TA cannot override fundamentals, but a single fundamental catalyst can instantly destroy an otherwise strong chart — always identify the next major binary catalyst for a position and understand which way the probabilities are skewed before relying on a technical setup (AGE, referencing BOE/Boss Energy as the cautionary precedent)

  • Continued explainer (deferred from last session) on the December share consolidation that confused holders — a genuinely routine ASX mechanic, not a red flag, and shareholders typically get advance notice/a vote

  • Reasons companies consolidate: simplifies the capital structure for a potential takeover, reduces share-price volatility for large institutional holders managing big positions (small pip moves matter less at a higher nominal price), and can make a stock more attractive to big funds that need "meaningful" per-share pricing to invest (parallel drawn to the uranium majors like BOE/PDN/DYL previously being the only index-eligible options)
  • Common pattern flagged: small-cap consolidations often see a short-term price drift down afterward as pip-traders (who rely on tiny 1-2 cent moves) exit, since the strategy no longer works at higher nominal prices — cites JAV's own consolidation as a recent example of this exact pattern

Session Themes

  • Capital raises remain part and parcel of resource/biotech investing — the key skill is checking cash position/upcoming spend before entering a position so a raise doesn't blindside you, not avoiding raise-prone sectors altogether

Session Themes

  • Capital raises are structurally normal, not a red flag, for pre-revenue exploration/development-stage resource and biotech companies — check the quarterly's Appendix 5B cash flow statement to confirm whether inflows are from equity issuance versus real operating receipts before reacting to a raise
  • Stage-based investing: understanding which stage (exploration, development, production) a resource company sits in tells you what catalysts, cash flow, and risk to expect — framed as a core Fund 101 concept

  • Metallurgical test work (not resource size) is repeatedly flagged as the critical unlock for rare earth developers specifically, since recoveries are deposit-specific and rarely transfer cleanly between projects (AXL)

  • Craig avoids setting hard target market caps for his own positions, since a fixed number can create anchoring/rationalisation bias when the underlying story changes (JAV)

Session Themes

  • Equivalent grades vs straight grades: a recurring caution that "equivalent" resource/assay figures can overstate the real content of the primary metal being marketed — always check what's actually blended into the calculation (LDR)
  • Assay intercepts vs full resource grade: narrow high-grade assay hits are not representative of the eventual MRE once waste/dilution between veins is included — wait for the full resource estimate before over-reacting to headline intercepts
  • Capital discipline in project development: smaller, staged builds funded from early production are repeatedly favoured over "world-class scale" mega-projects with huge CapEx/NPV headlines, which are more likely to dilute holders and lose pricing power before reaching cash flow (VAR vs ARU contrast)
  • Reading buried disclosures: tucking updated financial metrics inside a routine quarterly rather than a standalone announcement is treated as a signal management isn't confident the market will like the numbers (ARU)
  • China's structural control over specialty-metal processing (gallium, germanium, antimony): geopolitical headlines about supply-chain diversification are not the same as a near-term trading opportunity, since China has repeatedly flooded markets (nickel, lithium, rare earths) to destroy competing project economics once capital piles in
  • Detaching emotion from analysis: stocks that become "identity-linked" for holders (ARU) make it harder to assess risk objectively — strong personal conviction is not the same as a strong investment case
  • Regional exploration cycles: previously neglected jurisdictions (Tasmania this week, following the Gawler Craton and north Queensland recently) are coming back into focus as improving metal prices make previously uneconomic deposits viable again
  • Reading company announcements directly: reiterated as the baseline habit for avoiding confusion (LOT's consolidation) and catching real signals early (ALA's FDA filing date)

Session Themes

  • Net takeaway: bullish uranium globally, but explicitly not expecting Australia to move quickly on approvals/mining

Session Themes

  • Special joint session with guest macro investor Tung Nguyen on generational wealth transfer and its market implications, rather than the standard ticker-by-ticker FA scan
  • Generational wealth transfer thesis: a large wave of capital moving from boomers to Gen X/millennials over the next ~15 years is expected to bifurcate the economy given uneven financial literacy, and could structurally advantage newer platforms (Robinhood) over incumbents (Charles Schwab) as legacy account balances eventually flow to younger, platform-sticky users
  • ESG/impact investing flows expected to accelerate as capital shifts toward millennials/Gen Z, who show markedly higher ESG preference (~70%) than boomers/Gen X
  • India framed as the next long-duration structural growth story (median working age ~28 vs an aging China), a bullish read-through for iron ore/steel demand over a 10-15 year horizon, tempered by India's more bureaucratic, democratic decision-making pace versus China's centralised model
  • Position-sizing/conviction framework: position size should scale with depth of research/conviction in a thesis, not the reverse — illustrated by Tung holding a 7-figure silver position through a 10% single-day drawdown without panic
  • Style vs conviction: both hosts stressed finding one's own single method rather than chasing others' styles, and letting position size reflect genuine understanding — echoed via the Buffett "avoided tech for decades, then concentrated in Apple" example

  • Used as the direct comparator to LKE to illustrate a mispriced pair: trades only ~$100M above LKE despite being fundamentally much stronger

VUL Bearish 00:09:29

  • Craig's fundamental view: never been a fan, sees it as "overvalued like crazy"

  • General guidance given: understand the project's real timeline and manage position sizing/risk accordingly rather than holding on hope
GGA Neutral 00:56:24

CAZ Bullish 00:56:24
  • Cazaly Resources (~$15M market cap) sits directly next to GGA's Comet Vale ground; Craig maps the same Northwest-trending fault structures that control the Comet Vale gold running directly onto Cazaly's tenements
  • Frames this as geological pathfinding, not just proximity speculation — early drill holes on Cazaly's ground have already hit gold along the same structural corridor/shear zone as Paddington and the Super Pit
  • Thesis: when GGA's MRE drops (expected within the week) and confirms the scale/grade improvement, attention should flow to CAZ as the under-the-radar name on the same trend
  • Flagged as a name "no one's really watching" at this valuation given the read-through from GGA's news flow

Session Themes

  • Post-tax IRR (not headline pre-tax IRR) and CapEx-per-unit-of-production as the real filters for judging whether a feasibility study is actually attractive, not just whether the project is big
  • Distrust of staged CapEx disclosure that hides the true total cost (Chalice) versus companies that lay CapEx out by phase transparently (Galan)
  • Relative-value technique: compare market caps of similarly-staged peer companies to spot which one the market has mispriced (LKE vs GLN)
  • Geological pathfinding — using known fault/structural trends to identify under-the-radar juniors sitting on the same geology as a well-known, about-to-catalyse neighbour (GGA/CAZ)
  • Trading psychology: "stop trying to make money, execute your strategy" — money is the byproduct of disciplined execution, not chasing FOMO
  • Risk of holding through M&A uncertainty; don't expect the share price to run to deal value until the deal goes binding (STO example)
  • Long-running skepticism of "critical minerals" narratives dependent on Chinese supply control (nickel, lithium, rare earths, antimony, gallium) — China has a decades-long track record of flooding markets to destroy competing projects once the West invests

  • Craig described his personal investing style in contrast to a small-cap-portfolio approach used by another MtM educator (Dave): Craig runs concentrated micro/small-cap positions based on fundamentals (valuation, catalysts, over/undervaluation), rather than broad diversified small position sizing without a fundamental valuation lens — framed as neither approach being "right," just different styles that make up the wider MtM community.
  • Reiterated his "A1 setup" mine-restart strategy explicitly by name: tiny market cap, large historical sunk capital, known resource, low incremental cost to restart — described as a repeatable, high-conviction pattern he returns to "time and time again."

Session Themes

  • Reiterated look-through analysis technique: compare a company's market cap against its cash plus any listed equity stakes it holds, to spot situations where the market is effectively giving no credit to the core business or growth optionality.
  • Oil & gas-specific operational risk flagged generally: shutting in and restarting wells (for maintenance, tie-ins, etc.) carries real risk of wells not flowing properly again — treated as a distinct risk category from mineral exploration, which Craig considers comparatively "easier and more certain."
  • Single-project concentration risk (via AEL): a company with only one major growth lever, however promising, is treated as fundamentally riskier than one with multiple paths to a re-rate — worth distinguishing "great trading vehicle" from "long-term conviction holding" for names in this position.
  • Metallurgical test work repeatedly named as the single most important swing factor for any deposit combining an unusual pair of metals (e.g. silver-antimony) where there isn't an established peer group to benchmark recoveries against.

FA in Practice: Meet the MD of GLN, Galan Lithium

GLN Bullish Timestamp not available
  • Guest: JP Vargas de la Vega, founder and Managing Director of Galan Lithium — started the company with just $15,000 after quitting his job as a mining analyst to buy ground at the Hombre Muerto salt flat in Argentina; built it into what's described as the world's ninth largest lithium resource in development or production (9.6Mt LCE).
  • GLN is emerging as the only ASX-listed lithium developer targeting production in 2026 — fully funded through to construction completion, with construction 85% complete and a nanofiltration plant arriving from Australia in early 2026; targeting production by mid-2026.
  • Holds an export production permit, a feat JP says has only been achieved by one other lithium company in Argentina; also received Argentina's RIGI permit, locking in 30 years of fiscal stability and reduced tax rates.
  • Located directly adjacent to major players Rio Tinto and POSCO at the same salt flat.
  • Operating model: evaporation ponds for brine concentration, transitioning to nanofiltration technology to simplify production; JP laid out the case for lithium chloride production over traditional spodumene — higher grades, fewer processing steps, and better positioning for the growing LFP battery market currently dominated by Chinese manufacturers.
  • This ties directly to Craig's own standing pick within the lithium sector (confirmed as his single lithium holding in the 11 Nov session) — this guest session is the deeper follow-up explaining why.

Session Themes

  • Founder-origin story as a due-diligence angle: GLN wasn't spun out of an existing mining company or built on already-known ground — it exists because JP personally sourced and negotiated for the land, which Craig frames as a genuinely different (and telling) company origin versus typical ASX lithium juniors.
  • Fiscal/regulatory permitting (Argentina's RIGI regime, export production permit) treated as a hard differentiator versus peers still working through approvals — de-risks the path to first production.
  • Product-type distinction reinforced again: lithium chloride/carbonate production has a different cost and quality profile to spodumene concentrate, relevant to how a company is positioned for LFP battery demand specifically.

  • DroneShield's sell-off traced to a cluster of coinciding events: three insiders sold effectively their entire ordinary shareholdings (~$49M, ~$12M and ~$5M worth) within days of each other, keeping only unvested options — done via an uncontrolled on-market dump rather than a block trade, which needlessly destroyed both the share price and shareholder confidence.

  • Competitive risk: a similarly named US competitor was acquired by a large company that reportedly spends ~$400M/year on R&D versus DroneShield's ~$30-40M — a gap Craig believes DroneShield can't close in 5-10 years.
  • Valuation was already "disgustingly overvalued" (multi-billion dollar market cap against ~$20-25M annual revenue) before any of this; Craig reads the pattern of events (insiders cashing out right before technology and leadership problems became public) as suspicious, even while noting correlation isn't causation. Session Themes

  • Long-run macro thought experiment: a large intergenerational wealth transfer (older men's concentrated wealth passing to surviving spouses, and to a rising cohort of high-net-worth women investors) could meaningfully shift capital flows over the next 5-10 years, given data showing female investors trend toward longer holding periods and companies with stronger social/environmental stewardship — flagged as a factor not to ignore alongside ESG and commodity supercycle thinking, even though not yet fully researched.
  • Trade discipline example (via ILT): know specifically why you're in a position (a catalyst, a latent-value gap) and exit when that specific thesis is realised, even if you still like the underlying company long-term — don't let "it's still a good project" become a reason to abandon your original plan.
  • Repeated pattern: find deep, unpriced value (e.g. a large resource on a tiny market cap) before the market notices, then let the market's own re-rating do the work once the news catches up — rather than chasing stories the market has already priced in.
  • Reiterated equivalent-resource literacy: always check the underlying grade of the primary metal behind a headline "X-equivalent" resource figure before assuming a company's story matches its marketing.

  • Framing: BPT has always been a good trading stock; the interesting shift is that it may now also be developing genuine FA substance behind the technicals for the first time in years — worth watching over the next quarter or two to see if the improvement is consistent.
ARD Neutral 00:56:16
  • Noted a deliberate language shift in ARD's own announcements/presentations over the last month or two: moving from describing itself purely as a "silver" project to "silver polymetallic" project/deposit.
  • Craig reads this positively as more honest and representative — the deposit contains meaningful lead, zinc and gold alongside silver, and it's the combination (not silver alone) that likely makes the project economically viable, especially given Australian silver grades are typically low on their own.
  • Flags the importance of understanding "equivalent resource" reporting (e.g. silver-equivalent) before trusting headline resource figures in any polymetallic story — a company can present the same underlying resource very differently depending on how it's framed.
  • Also notes a newly floated idea of a small, easy-to-mine oxide starter pit for early cash flow (a pattern also seen in gold projects) — reads the combined shift (repositioning + starter-pit idea) as a sign of an internal strategic rethink, possibly prompted by major shareholders, and views it as a good-faith move toward a more viable long-term project.

Session Themes

  • Context is everything: a technically strong announcement (e.g. NIM's high-grade MRE) can still be sold down hard if it fails to clear the specific expectation the company itself set (e.g. via a prior exploration target) — judge announcements against their own stated benchmarks, not in isolation.
  • Reporting quality as a genuine differentiator: companies that clearly break out AISC/C1/AIC costs in both per-ton and per-pound terms save investors real analytical work and are called out as being shareholder-friendly; some larger, well-known peers report deliberately opaquely because they're serving brokers/financiers, not retail.
  • "Bigger company = safer" is explicitly rejected — company risk is proportional to complexity and what's actually happening inside it, not company size; multi-asset companies carry their own layered risks (funding multiple projects at once) that single-asset juniors don't.
  • Reiterated why net operating cash flow from a single asset isn't the same as whole-company financial health once corporate overhead and other project development spend are included.
  • Mining conference culture/etiquette: at industry conferences, watch for company reps who cluster in insular internal conversations vs. those who stay open to engaging outside investors — read as a signal about how shareholder-focused (or not) a management team actually is; also flagged informal/social-setting conversations as a genuinely useful source of context and color beyond what's in official announcements.
  • Equivalent-resource literacy flagged again as essential before taking any polymetallic story's headline grade/resource figure at face value.

  • Post-recapitalisation names: pre-recap chart/technical history is treated as void once share structure and company scope fundamentally change (e.g. AR1 absorbing Rocklands) — need fresh trading data before technicals become meaningful again.

Session Themes

  • General resource-acquisition logic (via MAN and BOE): companies near production prefer to acquire resources that are close to production-ready rather than starting from scratch, since a multi-year drill-out timeline often isn't viable against near-term production needs.

SHN Neutral 00:45:29 (case study / retrospective, not a fresh call)
  • Used as a worked example of the FA process — walks through how Craig identified Sunshine (SHN) around March 2025 (~$12-16M market cap) before its ~400% run.
  • Team pedigree was a key signal: Damien (structural geologist with Spectrum/Black Cat/Silver Lake/Gold Fields background), Paul (ex-Black Cat/DRE), Mika and Les — all linked to companies with strong exploration track records.

  • General lesson drawn: "a rising tide lifts all boats" is true short-term for a whole sector, but picking the highest-quality name in the group (not just anything cheap) compounds into materially larger gains over a longer hold.

Session Themes

  • Pullback psychology: don't fear a retest of a level you were hoping to buy at — that's how the market is supposed to work; check whether your original thesis is still intact rather than reacting emotionally to short-term red.
  • Breakout quality filter: only trust a breakout backed by an actual fundamental reason for revaluation (confluence between FA and TA) — chasing every technical breakout without that backing leads to repeated fakeouts.
  • "Square up" chart pattern explained: after a large explosive move/gap, market makers may guide price back to balance their order books, creating a visually "squared" range on the chart — a technical concept worth understanding, not a fundamentals signal on its own.
  • Governance/ownership red flags (via BEZ): large-holder funding delays, boardroom stacking via special meetings, and shifting voting blocks are material risk factors distinct from underlying asset quality; jurisdiction-specific voting rules (e.g. Canada's 30-day share-holding requirement) can explain otherwise-unexplained share price volatility ahead of a shareholder vote.
  • FA process worked example (via SHN): start from a company's own investor presentation for flagship project and management pedigree; cross-check resource size against market cap for mismatches; value clear, consistent catalyst communication from management as a quality signal.
  • Mine-safety incident (company referred to as "Poll" in the transcript — likely a mis-transcribed name, ticker not confirmed): trading halted after a serious incident; Craig deliberately declined to speculate on share price impact out of respect for those affected, and advised waiting for official company updates rather than news reports before drawing conclusions.
  • Announcements: FA 101 course opens for Term 1 2026 enrolments this Thursday (Craig's birthday); TYP CEO Jason and former Besra director David Potter both scheduled as guests the next day.

Session Themes

  • Commodity super-cycle backdrop: strong recent run with pullback "jitters" — volatility easing doesn't equal newfound stability; watch fund flows into defensive assets vs selective mining/energy risk appetite.
  • Liquidity Trap: thinly-traded rallies can reverse fast — use volume confirmation before trusting a breakout, on both entries and exits.
  • Catalysts vs. noise: maintain a "Catalyst Journal" — record what triggered a move, how price responded, and whether conviction followed through.
  • Institutional footprints: off-market/no-news volume spikes and unusual buying often precede news flow — use Level 2/broker depth to spot rotation early.
  • Risk framework restated: cash is a position; structure before story; volume confirmation; scale on confirmation not conviction; review losing trades monthly (thesis vs timing vs execution).
  • Takeover-offer evaluation method: price against the 30-day VWAP, not spot; check how the price actually got there (was it driven by the bidder's own buying?); read the bidder's rationale statement to judge intent.
  • Development financing tells: a revised study with updated metal prices ahead of a deal closing, and a large debt facility relative to market cap, both signal lender/acquirer confidence; importance of a locked-in offtake agreement and 10-year+ mine life for debt funding to work.
  • Announcements: FA 101 course opens for Term 1 2026 enrolments on 30 Oct 2025; TYP CEO guest session scheduled for 29 Oct.

FA in Practice: RR1 - Meet CEO Jeremy Bower of Reach Resources

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Friday 12 September 2025

RR1 (Reach Resources) Bullish Timestamp not available
  • CEO interview format: Craig hosted Jeremy Bower, CEO of Reach Resources, a former lithium explorer now transitioning toward small-scale gold production
  • Feasibility study update: the original scoping study was upgraded to a full feasibility study given the project's stage (pit design, ore body characteristics) — Jeremy wanted accuracy beyond what a scoping study's low confidence level allows; share price has risen since a June presentation
  • Strategic pivot from lithium to gold was market-driven: gold prices rising while lithium prices fell. Jeremy previously worked lithium ground in WA (Morrissey Hill, and Red Dirt which became Delta Lithium) but drill programs were hampered by falling lithium prices
  • On the retained lithium project: Delta earned 80%, RR1 received $3.2m upfront, with a requirement to spend $3m by March next year to reach 51% ownership
  • Rare earth project: initial pegmatite hypothesis was wrong — turned out to be an alkaline granite-hosted ore body, grading ~0.7% (similar to clay-style rare earth deposits), with higher grades found in weathered zones near faults; parked temporarily due to funding constraints, but ongoing internal work and university collaboration continues
  • Lean operation: only two employees, remote team, consultants brought in as needed, deliberately diversified across lithium/rare earths/manganese/gold to manage risk; strong financial position with share price of 1.2-1.3c and no debt
  • Resource classification discussion: moving from inferred to indicated resource requires closer drill spacing; pit designs evolve materially from scoping study (simplified optimised pit shells) to feasibility study, with ore loss/dilution a key consideration for narrow gold veins
  • Development progress: extensive cost analysis done via tenders and a partnership with Mine Build Global; native title, Aboriginal Heritage Act compliance, and flora/fauna surveys completed; strategy shifted to a 4-pit approach with 1.5 pits identified as rapid-development starter pits
  • Pansy Pit (drilled to 60m) shows geology similar to the Blue Heaven deposit (drilled to 200m), suggesting expansion potential; a diamond drilling program is planned to further assess mineralisation
  • Target to begin mining operations around June next year, starting with the Blue Heaven pit before expanding to Pansy and other deposits, pending mill readiness and approvals

Session Themes

  • Format was a direct CEO interview rather than Craig's usual multi-ticker scan — used as a live example of applying fundamental analysis to a company mid-transition (lithium explorer moving into gold production)
  • Recurring theme: the value of getting real production cash flow started (toll mining) while still building out the broader resource base, rather than purely drill-and-report
  • Emphasis on accuracy of study level (scoping vs feasibility) and resource classification (inferred vs indicated) as key diligence points investors should understand before trusting headline numbers
  • Regulatory/heritage permitting flagged as a real timeline and cost risk, with Jeremy noting frustration at slow progress on red-tape reduction despite years of promises

FA in Practice: Meet the MD and CEO of ALA (Arovella Therapeutics)

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Friday 29 August 2025
Bullish Setups: ALA (Arovella Therapeutics)
Bearish Setups: None
Neutral / Watching: None
ALA (Arovella Therapeutics) Bullish Timestamp not available
  • Developing an "off the shelf" allogeneic CAR-iNKT cell therapy for blood and solid tumour cancers: batch-manufactured from healthy donor cells and ready within 1 week, vs traditional autologous CAR-T which is manufactured per-patient and takes 3-4 weeks.
  • M&A backdrop flagged by Craig as the key thesis driver: all but one big-pharma buyout of small biotechs in this space since 2021 happened at the pre-clinical-to-Phase-1 stage — ALA is targeting the start of its Phase 1 trial in early 2026, putting it into that acquisition-interest window.
  • Balance sheet: ~$21M cash, plus potential further inflows from R&D tax incentives and option exercises; largest shareholders include Biotech Capital Management and Summit Biotech (institutional/strategic backing).
  • Pipeline: lead asset ALA-101 (blood cancer) targeting IND submission and Phase 1 dose-escalation trial start in early 2026 (4 dose levels, 9-12 patients in the first cohort, ~2 years to recruit ~30 patients total); trial budgeted at ~$15M, partly offset by R&D tax incentives.
  • Preclinical animal data comparing CAR-NKT to CAR-T showed 60% survival at 90 days for CAR-NKT vs 40-60% for other treatments; a neuroblastoma patient case using CAR-iNKT achieved a complete response — Michael (CEO) caveated that animal studies can't definitively predict human outcomes but support proceeding to clinical trials.
  • IP position: granted patents in Europe, Canada, Australia and Hong Kong; US patent still pending and considered critical. IP was initially licensed from universities rather than developed in-house; solid-tumour pipeline developed in collaboration with the University of North Carolina, with new CAR technology work ongoing with Baylor College of Medicine.
  • Manufacturing is outsourced to contract development/manufacturing organisations (CDMOs) rather than an in-house facility; clinical advisory board includes experts from successful CAR-T programs to help shape trial design. IL-12 TM technology in development could offer up to a 10x increase in circulating cell persistence.

Session Themes

  • How to evaluate a clinical-stage biotech fundamentally: patent position/geography, cash runway plus non-dilutive funding sources (R&D tax incentives), preclinical data quality, and where a company sits in the pre-clinical-to-Phase-2 "M&A window" that big pharma tends to buy into.
  • Communication quality as a signal: discussion of how companies sometimes use complex language to obscure a lack of real progress, versus clear, simple reporting being a positive sign.

SS1 (Sunsilver) Bearish 21:24 (revisited in detail at 32:49 re: misleading announcements)
  • Cap raise done at a 15% discount, ~$160M market cap for a large but low-grade (~60g/t silver-equivalent, using antimony/gold to boost the "equivalent" figure) resource — nothing new/unknown, so no speculative re-rate upside, and the raise triggered shareholder frustration/selling.
  • Flagged two announcements as among the most misleading Craig has seen: one implied 65m at 7.8% antimony in the headline, but the real interval was 44m @ 0.1% and 21m @ 0.11% — the 7.8% figure came from just a 9cm (0.09m) sub-interval, an example of "grade smearing" a tiny high-grade slice across a much larger, much lower-grade interval.
  • A second announcement's "51.4g/t silver, high-grade mineralisation" headline used a silver-equivalent grade (blending in gold/antimony) to dress up what is actually a low true silver grade — genuine primary silver deposits should show 200g/t+ (ideally 400g/t+) per the First Majestic FA in Practice benchmark; SS1 doesn't come close.
  • Craig's takeaway: stage of company (known/de-risked development vs. genuine exploration/discovery) heavily determines how the market reacts to a capital raise and to news flow generally.
SMM (Somerset Minerals) Bullish 46:19
  • Early-stage copper explorer; standout first hole of 42m @ 2.69% Cu — an exceptional grade for a maiden discovery result.
  • Recently raised $4M, roughly half its market cap, to fund follow-up; more assay results due in the coming weeks — high-risk but high-potential early discovery play.
TGM (Theta Gold Mines) Bullish 57:37
  • Restarting historical underground gold mines in South Africa; existing resource base of 6.1Moz gold.
  • $35M cornerstone funding secured from the IDC (Industrial Development Corporation) — a significant institutional validation for the project.
  • DFS update due shortly, expected to materially improve project economics at current gold prices; heavily held by top-20 institutional investors with Chinese influence in the register, raising potential for future strategic/takeover interest.

Session Themes

  • Don't chase "the next shiny object" — Craig opened by warning against jumping between hot sectors (silver, uranium, tech) without a clear strategy; real wealth comes from positioning early in undervalued sectors and holding through the full cycle.
  • Capital raise context matters: premium vs. discount pricing, and exploration/discovery-stage vs. known/development-stage, together explain why the market reacts so differently to two raises on the surface (WCE vs. SS1).
  • Craig's methodology for spotting misleading ASX announcements: watch for "up to" wiggle-room language, non-representative re-assay samples, "grade smearing" (a tiny high-grade sub-interval blended into a much larger low-grade interval), and silver/metal "equivalent" grades used to dress up genuinely low-grade results.
  • FA 101 (Fundamental Analysis Foundations) course has launched; upcoming FA in Practice sessions flagged for 29 Aug (Arabella/Michael, biotech) and 12 Sept (Jeremy, Reach Resources/RR1).

PGO (Pac Gold) Bullish 00:15:36

  • Craig used MIN vs. BOE as a teaching contrast: BOE's problem (wrong geology/grade) can't be fixed; MIN's problems (haul road, debt) are fixable in principle, which is the key difference for holders of either.

  • The Onslow haul road is still the critical swing factor — trucks are now running lighter loads (260t vs a 330t design spec) via bypass routes; throughput has improved but the road remains unproven at full nameplate (35Mtpa target).
  • Flagged a drop in transparency in the latest quarterly vs the prior one (dropped haulage breakdowns, switched from metric tons to wet metric tons) as a deliberate red flag — "there's a reason why you hide that."
  • Balance-sheet levers being discussed by management: selling the carry loan on the Onslow JV, selling the remaining half of the haul road, or divesting/scaling back lithium assets (currently ~NPV 0, loss-making/breakeven).
  • Craig's take: genuine two-way bet ("could go to $10 or to $50") — advises extreme caution given how much is still unknown, including true per-tonne costs.
NVX Bearish 00:57:16
  • Deep dive on Novonix's US$100M financing deal with Yorkville (convertible debentures in tranches), taken from a position of weakness after offtake delays and ~$20-25M/quarter cash burn.
  • Structure heavily favours Yorkville: effective 5% instant discount, conversion floor of 12c and ceiling of 64c (so NVX shares are not "worth $1-1.40" as some retail chatter suggested), plus negative covenants giving Yorkville veto rights over any other debt/financing NVX wants to raise.
  • Later tranches are conditional — outstanding debentures must stay under 20% of market cap and average daily traded value must stay above $600k over 20 of any 30 trading days — meaning funding can evaporate if the share price or liquidity falls.
  • Craig has never rated NVX's fundamentals (overpromising, under-delivery, poor planning); sees Magnus in a similar position; calls NVX "a house of cards that's been on fire" — this deal buys time, but one hiccup could unwind it.
  • First offtake supply obligations (Panasonic/LG) due around September — a key near-term test of whether the raise actually buys enough runway.

Session Themes

  • Two methodology threads dominate the session: (1) how to judge exploration-stage juniors by team pedigree plus systematic, staged target generation rather than rushing to drill; (2) how to properly stress-test a distressed balance sheet (liquidity, net debt, EBITDA, transparency) using MIN as the live case study.
  • Extended breakdown of convertible debenture mechanics (floor/ceiling conversion prices, negative covenants, drawdown conditions) using NVX's Yorkville deal as a teaching example — how such deals can look like "free money" headlines but hide dilution/control risk.
  • Craig flagged reduced quarterly reporting transparency (MIN) as a red flag worth actively watching for across any company.
  • Housekeeping: FA in Practice with Michael from ALA (Arovella Therapeutics) scheduled for Aug 29; new FA101 course launching soon (waitlist mentioned).

FA in Practice: Meet First Majestic Silver

Hosted by Craig Dickson | Friday 04 July 2025
Bullish Setups: First Majestic Silver (AG), Silver
Bearish Setups: None
Neutral / Watching: None
First Majestic Silver (AG) Bullish 00:01:07
  • Special guest interview with Mani Alkhafaji, VP Corporate Development at First Majestic Silver (~US$4-5.5B market cap silver producer), a decade of experience across finance/operations including years on the ground at the company's Mexican mine sites.
  • Core production: ~15M oz silver annually (~30M oz silver-equivalent) across 4 underground mines in Mexico; ~85% of production is precious metals (60% silver, 30% gold, balance zinc/lead). Average grade ~150-200 g/t silver, with some assets up to 800-1,000 g/t silver-equivalent.
  • Los Gatos acquisition (Gatos Silver) — 00:06:48: won after a competitive 13-bidder process; sits in the lowest global cost quartile, high-grade/long-life with modern infrastructure, and immediate production synergies already realised.
  • Exploration strategy prioritises brownfields over greenfield risk — Santa Elena land package alone is ~102,000ha with continuous discovery since 2015 (00:27:08); annual depletion of 10-12M oz is replenished via sustained drilling; ~270km of drilling planned for 2025.
  • Fast-track development edge: existing infrastructure let them bring the Navidad deposit to production in ~3 years vs. the ~18-year industry-average discovery-to-production timeline.
  • Vertical integration via its own Las Vegas minting facility (00:02:01) — the only public silver producer globally with an in-house mint; sells ~7% of production direct to consumers at $3-5/oz premiums over spot; strategic rationale is pulling physical silver out of paper-market circulation and capturing full value-chain margin (collectible/branded coin lines). Long-term goal: mint all of First Majestic's own silver and eventually offer minting as a service to other producers.
  • Balance sheet: ~$500M cash, minimal (USD-denominated) debt; single-day trading volumes have hit ~$750M. Buybacks (00:45:19) used opportunistically when the stock is seen as undervalued; dividend (00:50:53) is modest (~1% of revenue) but framed as scalable.
  • Some cash is restricted, tied to reclamation funds and a pending San Dimas streaming tax dispute in Mexico (00:36:25) — resolution expected within ~12 months, which would unlock further liquidity.
  • M&A discipline: organic drilling prioritised over acquisitions; any M&A must be high-grade, expandable, low-cost and jurisdictionally aligned — open to further growth in US/Canada/Australia (an Australian visit is planned for early 2026) but explicitly avoiding higher jurisdictional-risk regions like Argentina or Bolivia (00:02:54 / 01:02:54).
  • Exploration team is experimenting with AI tools for target modelling/geophysics (00:56:18) — early days, but management wants to stay on the innovation frontier, consistent with prior early adoption of technologies like high-intensity grinding mills.
  • Heavy, centrally-managed (Vancouver) CSR spend on education/healthcare/water/agriculture in mining communities, structured so budgets aren't cut during downturns — framed as a long-term social-licence differentiator.
Silver (Commodity) Bullish 00:04:24
  • Structural deficit thesis: annual mined supply (~1B oz) can't keep up with demand (especially industrial/electrification use); recycling/secondary supply insufficient to close the gap; average 18-year mine discovery-to-production lag structurally limits new supply.
  • Gold-to-silver price ratio currently ~90:1 (00:04:24/00:04:38) versus a mining (extraction) ratio of only ~7:1 — used as the key evidence that silver is significantly undervalued relative to gold.
  • "Paper vs. physical" distortion (00:10:00): each physical ounce is estimated to trade 200-250 times in paper markets, creating "illusory liquidity" that suppresses the real price of physical silver — cited as First Majestic's own motivation for building out its mint.
  • Price outlook: the 2011 inflation-adjusted high (~US$65-70) is framed as the near-term bull target; management's own view is that triple-digit silver (00:04:38) is plausible if the gold-silver ratio compresses further and deficits persist.

Session Themes

  • Rare direct-from-management access: Craig hosted the VP of Corporate Development live rather than presenting third-party research, giving attendees an operator's-eye view of a large-cap silver producer.
  • Vertical integration (mining -> minting) as a distinct strategic lever for a producer to capture more of the value chain and reduce reliance on paper-market pricing.
  • Jurisdictional discipline in M&A screening — willingness to expand into stable jurisdictions (US/Canada/Australia) while explicitly ruling out higher-risk regions, regardless of asset quality.
  • Structural supply/demand and paper-vs-physical dynamics presented as the core long-term bull case for silver as a commodity, independent of any single equity.

  • When combined with doxorubicin, RC220 improves cancer-killing efficacy and cuts cardiac-ageing side effects from ~15 years down to 3-5 years — a major differentiator with no direct competitor doing the same heart-protection function.

RR1 (Reach Resources) Bullish 00:46:29
  • Craig previously followed RR1 in lithium; assays disappointed, but the company pivoted.
  • Now aggressively fast-tracking toward production at the Pansy gold deposit: skipping traditional PFS/DFS delays, going straight from scoping study to mining (targeted ~9 months of mining, expected to start ~Feb, possibly by year-end).

Session Themes

  • Value over price: every trade/hold decision should start from market cap and underlying value, not chart appearance — a recurring "Captain Planet" framework reminder (TA + FA + volume alignment).
  • Dilution timing as a distinct risk factor for capital-intensive resource stories (SGQ case study) — mark expected cap-raise windows in advance.
  • De-risked, repurposed/reformulated biotech assets (RAC) can meaningfully lower binary risk versus a typical clinical-stage biotech bet.
  • Permitted infrastructure (processing plants, offtake-ready gas assets) treated as a standalone value driver distinct from the resource itself.
  • Reminder to source company data directly from the ASX company announcements page rather than third-party finance sites/apps, which are often outdated or inaccurate.
